body: Production migrations roll forward, never back. Backwards migrations exist in the tree and get used freely on laptops, but running one against production is treated as an incident action requiring a second engineer in the channel. That standing decision came out of the night someone reversed a column rename using the generated down step and lost four hours of shipment status writes, because the reverse of a rename that already has traffic on it is not a rename. What replaced rollback is expand/contract. Every schema change ships as an additive migration first, and the destructive half — dropping the old column, tightening the constraint — lands in a separate release at least one deploy later, so the running application is always compatible with both the previous and the next schema. `make migrate-check` runs `tools/migration_guard.py` in the pipeline and fails on DROP COLUMN, type alterations against populated tables, and index creation without CONCURRENTLY, unless the migration carries an explicit `reviewed_destructive = true` marker with a linked ticket. When a change genuinely has to be undone in production, the answer is a new hand-written forward migration reviewed by two people. Point-in-time restore is the last resort and is a full cluster restore, so it costs the whole database rather than one table. The planning consequence: any schema change needing a cleanup pass is two tickets from the start, not one.

Flag cleanup is enforced by the build, not by good intentions. Every flag is declared in `config/flags.yaml` with an owner, a ticket and a required `expires_on` date no more than ninety days out, and the loader refuses to boot if a flag is referenced in code but missing from that file. A nightly workflow runs `python -m tools.flag_audit`, which fails for any flag past its expiry with no open removal PR and posts the list into the owning team's channel. Removal is two deploys, always in the same order: flip the default in the config and ship it, let it sit through one full release cycle so reverting is still cheap, then delete the branches in code and drop the row from `feature_flags`. Skipping that wait is what produced the invoicing outage. A kill switch nobody had touched in two years was still wired into the settlement path, and someone tidying stale entries in the admin UI toggled it off mid-afternoon. That was the second incident traced to an abandoned flag, which is the point at which cleanup stopped being hygiene and became a gate. The heuristic that came out of the review: a flag whose expiry has been extended twice is not a flag, it is configuration, and it should either be promoted to a real setting or deleted outright.

The nightly backup job used to count as green if the snapshot API call returned zero. That belief cost us when WAL archiving broke silently for eleven days — snapshots were being taken, the dashboard stayed green, and the point-in-time recovery window we thought we had did not exist. Nobody noticed until an engineer tried to recover a dropped table and found the earliest restorable point was the previous week.

Since then, a backup is not considered taken until it has been restored. `ops/backup/verify_restore.sh` runs at 04:10 UTC, provisions a throwaway instance from the most recent automated snapshot, replays WAL to the newest available LSN, then runs three checks: `pg_restore --list` against the logical dump to confirm it parses, a row-count comparison on `shipments` and `tariff_versions` against production within a tolerance band, and a checksum over the previous day's closed ledger entries. The instance is destroyed at the end regardless of outcome.

The job emits `backup_restore_verified_age_seconds`, and the page fires when that exceeds 26 hours. The alert is deliberately on the verification's age, not the snapshot's — that distinction is the entire point of the rebuild. Do not silence it by re-running the snapshot; the snapshot was never the thing in doubt.

What the runbook says and what actually happens differ, and the difference is intentional. Written policy is: primary pages, fifteen minutes to auto-escalate to secondary, then the engineering manager. In practice the secondary is almost never paged by the tool — the primary opens the incident channel and pulls in whoever owns the failing service, and that person joins voluntarily, usually within a couple of minutes. Manager escalation is reserved for decisions that are not technical: getting a vendor's account team on the phone at night, deciding to accept data loss, deciding to wake an executive. The norms that came out of the bad night in spring and have held since: the primary's job is to declare, not to fix — nobody has ever been criticised for declaring early, and a few people have been criticised for waiting. Anyone can raise a severity; only the incident commander can lower it. Customer-facing comms go out at the thirty-minute mark whether or not there is a diagnosis, because during that outage the silence generated more inbound support volume than the outage did. And the schedule is authoritative for paging but not for reality — people swap shifts by saying so in the channel and often never update the tool, so when it matters who is actually awake, ask in the channel instead of trusting the rotation view.

Public API rate limiting lives at the edge gateway, not in the application, and is keyed on the API key rather than the source IP — customer integrations run behind NAT and shared egress, so IP buckets punished the wrong callers. Token bucket per key: `sustained_rate = 20` requests per second with `burst = 60`, configured in `services/gateway/ratelimit.yaml` and hot-reloaded without a deploy.

Those numbers came from measuring the p99 request rate of legitimate nightly batch jobs across the top twenty accounts and rounding up roughly 3x. They are not a capacity limit — the gateway saturates far above them — they are an abuse and runaway-loop limit, which is why raising one is routine rather than fraught.

Two carve-outs. The webhook replay endpoint gets its own much tighter bucket, because a customer retry storm there fans out into ledger writes. All sandbox keys share a single global bucket on purpose, so load testing against sandbox can never be mistaken for a production signal.

Rejected requests return 429 with Retry-After, and remaining budget is exposed on every response so integrators can pace themselves instead of discovering the wall.

Raising a ceiling is a config change plus a look at the gateway saturation panel first. We have never refused one, but twice the customer's real problem turned out to be polling a list endpoint instead of consuming webhooks, and we fixed that instead.

Decided in March and now the rule for everything on the cluster: application secrets arrive as files, never as environment variables. The external-secrets operator in the `platform-system` namespace reconciles one `ExternalSecret` per service against AWS Secrets Manager under `/kestrel/<env>/<service>/`, writes a native Kubernetes Secret, and the service's Helm chart mounts it as a projected volume at `/var/run/secrets/kestrel/`. Services read the file at point of use instead of caching it at boot, so a rotation propagates within the operator's `refreshInterval: 15m` with no rollout — that was the whole point of the migration, since the old pattern required a full redeploy to rotate anything and so nobody rotated. Env vars were rejected on specifics, not taste: they are inherited by every forked child, readable out of /proc by anything sharing the pid namespace, and we found database passwords verbatim in crash-reporter payloads twice last year. Second reason, and the one to cite when someone proposes a shared "app secrets" bundle again: each pod's service account assumes an IAM role scoped to its own prefix, so a compromised container cannot read another service's material. One exception still stands — the legacy invoicer reads its database password once during Rails initialisation, so it is injected at boot and rotating it there still means a restart. That exception disappears with the billing cutover, not before.

The review agreement, made at the retro after a quarter where the median pull request sat almost four days, is about first response and nothing else: a reviewer acknowledges within one business day, either taking it or handing it to someone who can. Acknowledgement is explicitly not approval, and the team deliberately refused to turn this into a measured SLA. The earlier dashboard experiment produced fast approvals with no comments inside them, which everyone agreed was worse than slow ones. Small changes, roughly under two hundred lines, are expected the same day. Large refactors are supposed to be arranged with a named reviewer before the branch opens, so nobody meets a two-thousand-line diff cold and then quietly avoids it for a week. Urgent production fixes skip blocking review entirely: pair with whoever is oncall, merge, review after the fact. The part that mattered most in practice turned out to be social rather than procedural. The author pings the channel once, and after that it is the reviewer's problem and not the author's, so chasing stopped feeling rude and people stopped accumulating stacks of dependent branches out of politeness.

Background jobs are named `domain.verb_object`, lowercase snake_case on both sides of the dot: `billing.retry_failed_charge`, `ledger.close_daily_period`, `notifications.send_invoice_email`. No `_job` or `_task` suffix — the registry already tells you what kind of thing it is. The domain segment is not decorative: the queue a job lands on is derived from it, so mislabeling the domain silently routes work to the wrong worker pool and the wrong alert route.

The pattern is enforced by a test that walks every key in `services/worker/registry.py` and matches it against the regex, so a badly named job fails CI instead of relying on someone catching it in review.

Treat a rename as a breaking change. Queued messages carry the job name as a plain string, so a deploy that renames without an alias will find in-flight messages with no handler and dead-letter them. The procedure is: register the new name, keep the old one as an alias for one full release, delete it once the queue has drained past the retention window.

The convention came out of an incident where two teams owned jobs whose names differed only by pluralization, and the on-call engineer paused the wrong one while working a backlog. A job name should tell you which team owns it and what it does to what, without opening the code.

The agreed shape of the invoicer retirement, out of the planning session with finance: dual-write first, then shadow reads, then per-tenant read flips, then a long read-only tail. No step skipped, and no date attached to any of them. Dual-write has to survive at least one full month-end close before anything else moves, because the rare proration and mid-cycle plan-change paths only execute at close; a week of weekday traffic proves nearly nothing about the code paths that are expensive when wrong. During shadow reads the diff report is the deliverable, not the migration itself — legacy stays authoritative, the new service computes in parallel, and every discrepancy gets explained rather than tuned away, because the legacy rounding behaviour is baked into signed contracts and "the new number is more correct" is not a defence anyone can take to a customer. Read flips go smallest tenant first, and finance holds the go/no-go, not engineering; their bar is two consecutive closes with an empty diff across the top revenue tier. Two standing constraints: no schema changes to the legacy database while parallel running is on, so that any diff is attributable; and rollback means pointing reads back at legacy, which only works while dual-write is still running. The day writes stop is the real point of no return — after that, rollback is a restore. The whole thing is gated on empty diffs rather than a date because date pressure on the last migration is exactly what produced the shortcuts we are still paying for.

We stopped using the monorepo in the spring, about eighteen months after adopting it. The reason was not a technical failure of the tooling — it was that the feedback signal had gone dead. With twenty engineers committing into one tree and no build graph, every pull request ran the full test matrix, which drifted from six minutes to over forty. People stopped reading CI results and started merging on the assumption that whatever was red belonged to somebody else's flake. That state is exactly what we had adopted the monorepo to avoid.

The alternative we weighed first was keeping the single tree and buying honest incrementality with a build-graph tool. We rejected it deliberately. A correct build graph is a standing maintenance obligation, and we have no platform team to carry it; choosing it would have meant one senior engineer permanently assigned to build infrastructure, which is a worse trade than the one we made.

So the tree was split into one repository per deployable service, with the shared domain models extracted into an internal library published as a versioned package. We went in with eyes open on the costs: cross-cutting changes now need coordinated pull requests in three or four places, version skew between services is possible and will eventually bite us, and atomic refactors across service boundaries are gone. Those are visible, occasional costs. A CI signal nobody trusts is an invisible, continuous one.

Adding a runtime dependency requires a written case in the pull request. Adding a development or test dependency does not. The case has to answer three things: what specifically breaks if we write the needed slice ourselves, who maintains the package upstream and how recently they shipped, and what removing it later would cost. Reviewers push hardest on the first question, because most proposed dependencies are being pulled in for a small fraction of what they actually do.

Anything touching money arithmetic, authentication, or the serialization of stored records needs two approvals instead of one. Those are the places where a quiet upstream behaviour change becomes a correctness bug that our tests will happily go green on.

The policy is deliberately not about install size or build time. Both come up in review and neither has ever blocked a change. It exists because a runtime dependency is a standing trust decision and an ongoing patching obligation, and the expensive moment is never the day you add it — it is two years later, discovering that an unmaintained package sits underneath the billing path and nobody remembers what it was chosen over. Vendoring a hundred lines with a comment recording where they came from is an accepted outcome and often the preferred one.

Retention on the self-hosted log stack is fourteen days and that is deliberate, not a leftover default. It was set during the storage review after the object-store bill for the logging cluster passed the compute bill for the entire staging environment; at ninety days of ingest the index alone was the third-largest line item and growing with traffic, while the query telemetry showed almost nothing reaching past six days. The second reason is the one that actually locks it in place: request logs carry shipper names, pickup addresses and partial consignment numbers, and the data-handling policy caps identifiable transit data at two weeks unless it passes through redaction. Nobody had the appetite to build and own a redaction pipeline purely so debug logs could live longer, so the shorter window answered both problems at once. Long-lived evidence lives elsewhere by design. The financial audit trail is a separate append-only store kept for seven years, and metrics and traces are downsampled and held for thirteen months, which covered both of the incidents where anyone genuinely needed older history. Standing guidance for whoever is oncall is to export the relevant window to the incident archive bucket while they are still responding, rather than asking to raise the global retention afterwards. That request has come up three times and been declined three times.

Force-pushing a shared branch is prohibited, and the rule dates from the afternoon `release/2409` lost three merged pull requests: someone rebased to tidy their own commits, did not notice their local ref was two days stale, and pushed over the branch. The reflog that saved us lived on exactly one laptop, and recovery ate an afternoon of a release freeze.

Force-push freely on branches nobody else has touched — your own `feat/*` work before review — and always with `--force-with-lease` rather than `--force`, because the lease turns losing a race into a rejected push instead of a silent overwrite. Never on `main`, anything under `release/*`, or a branch with an open pull request someone else has reviewed or built on. If shared history genuinely needs rewriting, open a new branch and a fresh PR rather than doing surgery in place.

Enforcement is doubled on purpose, because the policy alone did not hold: branch protection rejects non-fast-forward pushes to the protected patterns, and `.githooks/pre-push` catches the obvious cases before the network is touched. The hook only fires in clones that set `core.hooksPath`, which the bootstrap script does. The remote rule is the guarantee; the hook exists so the failure is fast and legible.

`ClientDisconnect` is filtered out of error tracking on purpose — the `before_send` hook in `services/api/observability.py` drops it before anything leaves the process. It is raised by the ASGI server whenever a caller hangs up mid-response, which for us means mobile clients on poor networks and load balancer probes timing out at an awkward moment. Nothing in that path is actionable: the request is already gone, and no state is left half-written because the transaction boundary closes before the response starts streaming.

The reason this is worth recording is volume. Before the filter it was roughly two thirds of all reported events, which pushed genuine regressions off the first page of the issue list and consumed the monthly event quota by about the third week.

Dropping it from error tracking is not dropping it from observability. The same exception still increments `http_client_disconnect_total`, and a sustained spike there is a real signal — usually an upstream proxy whose idle timeout is shorter than ours, which is exactly how the misconfigured edge timeout was found last winter.

There was a proposal to add `TimeoutError` to the same ignore list because it is also noisy. Rejected: those are our timeouts against our own dependencies, and they are precisely the thing we want to be woken up about.

The integration suite runs on a single worker deliberately: `make test-integration` shells out to `pytest tests/integration -n 0`, and CI passes the same flag. This is not an oversight and should not be "fixed" by turning workers back on. Every integration test shares one Postgres database, and the session fixture truncates all tables between tests; under xdist, one worker's truncation deleted rows another worker was mid-assertion on, which surfaced as roughly a four percent flake rate that people handled by re-running until green. That habit costs more than the eight minutes serial execution costs. Per-worker schemas were tried and abandoned — the rating engine resolves tenants through a materialised view whose refresh trigger hardcodes `public`, and two migrations install database-scoped extension objects that cannot be duplicated per schema. Doing it properly means making the search path configurable inside the rating engine, which is worth doing eventually and not worth doing to reclaim eight minutes of wall clock. Unit tests still run fully parallel; the serial constraint applies only to the database-backed suite.

Moved connection pooling out of the application processes and into a standalone PgBouncer deployment in September, after the second connection-exhaustion incident in a month. The app-side pools were the problem: each `dispatch-api` pod opened its own pool of 20, and the HPA happily scaled to 60 pods during the pre-holiday tender surge, so we asked for roughly 1200 backends against an RDS instance with `max_connections = 500`. Postgres does not degrade gracefully there — it refuses, the refusals landed on the healthcheck path, pods got killed, and the survivors scaled harder into the same wall.

PgBouncer now runs as its own deployment behind a ClusterIP service with `pool_mode = transaction` and a server pool sized to 180. Application pools were cut to 2 per process, which keeps latency flat because the client-side pool is now only absorbing thread contention, not connection setup.

The cost is real and worth naming: transaction pooling means no session state survives a statement boundary. We moved LISTEN/NOTIFY in the `ledger` worker onto a direct connection that bypasses the pooler, dropped server-side prepared statements in the Go services, and audited every `SET LOCAL` we depended on. Session-scoped advisory locks were rewritten as row locks. Anything that genuinely needs a session gets a documented direct-connect DSN — never a per-service exception carved into the pooler config.

The frontend build output is intentionally not cached in CI, and there is a comment saying so in `.github/workflows/web-ci.yml` because two different people have since tried to add it back. We cached the Vite output and `node_modules` for about three weeks in early spring and spent most of that time chasing ghosts. The cache key was the lockfile hash alone, but the bundle embeds the commit SHA and the API client generated from the schema at build time, so a fully green pipeline could ship chunks built against last week's types. Two of those reached production before anyone connected the symptoms to the cache. The payoff was small even when it behaved: cold build measured around 3m10s against 2m40s warm once the runners moved to the larger instance class, and restoring a 400 MB directory over the network ate most of that difference. What stayed is the package store cache keyed on `pnpm-lock.yaml`, which is content-addressed and cannot go stale the same way. If build time becomes painful again, the agreed direction is to split the CI job per workspace package and parallelise, not to reintroduce an output cache.

Staging runs against a single shared database on purpose; it is not an accident of neglect. We started with ephemeral per-branch databases seeded from fixtures. Two problems killed that: seeding a realistic freight dataset took most of half an hour, so people skipped staging entirely, and the fixtures slowly diverged from the shapes real customers produce. The bugs that actually reached production were almost never logic bugs the fixtures would have caught — they were data-shape bugs. The multi-leg shipment with a null intermediate stop. The tariff with an open-ended validity window. Synthetic seed data never had those.

Staging now points at one long-lived database restored weekly from a scrubbed production dump, and everyone shares it. We took the contention knowingly: engineers occasionally stomp each other's test records, migrations have to be sequenced rather than applied in parallel, and destructive tests are banned there — those belong on a local instance.

The framing that keeps this from becoming a mess is that staging is not a correctness gate. CI is the correctness gate, and CI still uses isolated per-run databases with fixtures. Staging answers one narrower question: does this behave sanely against data that looks like the real thing. Because that is its only job, one shared database is sufficient, and the fidelity of real-shaped data is worth more to us than isolation would be.

Every Dockerfile pins its base by digest — `FROM public.ecr.aws/docker/library/python:3.12-slim@sha256:<digest>` — and `scripts/check_base_digests.py` runs in the lint job, failing any FROM line without an `@sha256:` suffix. The reason is one specific outage: upstream retagged the slim image with a newer glibc, our tag-only pin silently picked it up during an unrelated rebuild, and the ledger service began segfaulting inside a compiled dependency in production six hours after an identical-looking build had passed staging. Tags are mutable, so a tag pin only means the artifact you tested and the artifact you shipped are probably the same image. A digest makes rebuilds reproducible and turns a base upgrade into a reviewed one-line diff with a changelog attached, rather than something that happens to you. Second reason, added later: the release gate matches the build attestation against the base digest, so an unpinned FROM breaks provenance verification outright. Maintenance cost stays low because the dependency bot opens the digest bump weekly — pinning buys determinism at the price of merging a PR, not at the price of vigilance.

Retired the shared development host in the second quarter and moved everyone to per-developer environments. The trigger was a half-applied schema migration that one engineer ran against the shared database on a Tuesday morning and left the entire backend team unable to boot the app until late afternoon; that was the third outage of the same class in a year. The deeper argument, and the one that actually settled it, is that a shared box makes every developer's environment a piece of production-shaped infrastructure nobody owns: it drifts from what is deployed, it accumulates hand-applied fixes that live in no repository, and it turns cheap local experiments into changes with a blast radius.

Someone proposed provisioning a second host so teams could split across them. We rejected that because capacity was never the constraint — shared mutable state was, and two hosts halve the pain rather than remove it.

The tradeoffs were accepted knowingly. Laptops are slower for the full integration stack, first-day setup takes longer, and a few people lost the convenience of a machine that was always warm. In exchange, a broken environment is now one person's problem and is fixed by throwing it away rather than by asking in chat whether anyone else is mid-migration. If reviving a shared box comes up again for cost reasons, the answer is no on isolation grounds, not on cost.

Architecture decisions live in each Alderpoint service repo under `docs/decisions/` as `NNNN-kebab-title.md` with a zero-padded four-digit prefix — `docs/decisions/0042-router-backpressure.md` is the shape. Numbers are allocated at PR time from one above the highest existing file, and they are never reused or renumbered, even when a decision is withdrawn a week later. Reversing a decision means writing a new ADR and adding `status: superseded-by-0057` to the front matter of the old one, which otherwise stays exactly as written. This rule came out of a bad quarter on the telemetry-router work: two accepted ADRs had been edited in place to match what the code had drifted into, so the files no longer explained the tradeoff that was actually made, and the team relitigated an argument it had already settled and lost once. The value of the decision log is the sequence of tradeoffs over time, not a description of the current system — the code already describes the current system, and does it better. Reviewers reject any ADR PR that mutates a prior decision's Decision or Consequences sections. Typo fixes, broken-link repairs and adding a supersession pointer are the only edits allowed to a merged ADR.

`scripts/docs_audit.py`, invoked as `make docs-audit`, lists handbook documents whose `reviewed:` date is more than 180 days old, grouped by owning team. The output is posted at the start of each cycle and it is advisory — no ticket is auto-created and nobody is required to act. That was a deliberate retreat from the earlier version, a quarterly documentation gardening day that produced a burst of cosmetic edits, a lot of `reviewed:` dates bumped without a read, and no measurable improvement. Making the list visible and cheap to ignore turned out to work better: teams pick off the two or three entries that embarrass them, and the rest of the list is honest evidence that we do not care about those pages, which is itself information. Twice now the sweep has been the thing that got a document deleted rather than updated, and that counts as a success.

Queue alerting fires on the age of the oldest message, not on depth: `rabbitmq_queue_head_message_age_seconds > 300` sustained for five minutes. Depth alerts failed us in both directions. Every bulk import legitimately pushes two hundred thousand messages and drains them in four minutes, so the depth alarm fired constantly and people muted it. Meanwhile the incident that actually cost us was a consumer wedged on a socket read with roughly nine hundred messages sitting untouched — far too shallow to trip anything, and we found out from a customer nine hours later. Head-message age measures the thing we actually care about, which is whether work is moving, and it is completely insensitive to how much work happens to be queued. We kept a very high depth alarm as a separate, lower-urgency signal for the runaway-producer case. The same principle now covers the SQS path through its approximate-age-of-oldest-message metric.

Tuned Alertmanager grouping and inhibition after a fifteen-minute regional network blip produced sixty-one separate notifications. The config now sets `group_by: [alertname, cluster, service]` with `group_wait: 45s` and `group_interval: 5m`, and an inhibit rule where a firing alert with `severity: critical` suppresses `severity: warning` alerts sharing the same `cluster` and `service` labels.

The forty-five second group wait is a deliberate trade: it delays the first notification by up to that long, which we judged acceptable because nothing here is resolvable in under a minute anyway, and it lets a cascading failure arrive as one message listing eight affected services rather than eight messages. The inhibition rule reflects how people actually behave — if a service is down, nobody needs to be told separately that its latency is elevated.

We considered inhibiting across services based on a dependency graph and rejected it. The graph would need maintaining, it would be wrong exactly when the architecture had changed, and a suppressed alert that should have fired is far more expensive than a redundant one. Inhibition stays within a single service, where the relationship is obvious and stable.

Adopted a rule that every alert must state, in its own text, what the responder should do first. Not a link to a runbook that may or may not exist, though a link is welcome too — an actual sentence in the alert body. The motivation was watching a new engineer receive a page about a metric threshold at two in the morning and spend eleven minutes working out what the metric even measured. Alerts that couldn't be given a first action were the interesting ones: about a fifth of our alert definitions turned out to have no answer to that question, which meant they were telling us something was unusual without telling us it was bad. Those got deleted or downgraded to a dashboard panel. The deletions were the real win. Alert volume dropped by roughly a third, and the remaining alerts became credible again, which matters more than the raw number — the failure mode we were actually in was that people had stopped believing pages meant anything. Nobody has proposed reversing this. The rule is now enforced by convention at review time rather than by tooling, and that has held up fine.

Every alert rule that can page must carry a `runbook_url` annotation pointing at a real page, and a `summary` written as a sentence describing impact. This is enforced, not encouraged: `scripts/check_alert_annotations.py` walks the rule files under `observability/rules/` and fails CI on any rule with `severity: critical` that lacks either annotation or whose runbook link 404s against the wiki API.

We added the link check after discovering three runbook URLs pointing at pages that had been moved a year earlier — the annotation was present, so the original lint passed, and the person who followed the link at three in the morning got nothing. The summary requirement exists because the default alert text was the rule name, and "HighErrorRateDispatch" tells you nothing about whether drivers can be assigned loads. The convention is that a summary must be understandable by someone who has never seen the service, which in practice means naming the user-visible consequence first and the metric second.

Writing the runbook before the rule merges also filters out a surprising number of proposed alerts. If nobody can describe what to do about it, it was never a page.

`#eng-announce` is post-only. Announcements go in as top-level messages; all discussion happens in the thread beneath, never in the channel. Each post must also be self-contained — if it says a thing has changed, it says what changed, when it takes effect, and who to ask, rather than linking to a document the reader must open to find out whether it concerns them. The rule exists because the channel had drifted into a general conversation space, people muted it, and then an actual announcement about a shared interface change reached about a third of engineering. A channel whose signal ratio drops gets muted, and a muted announcement channel is worse than none because senders still believe they have communicated. Anything that needs a decision does not belong here at all; it belongs in the owning team's channel or in a proposal document.

The public API reference is generated from `openapi/insights.yaml` by `make api-docs`; nobody hand-writes endpoint tables any more. CI runs the generator in check mode and fails if the committed output differs from a fresh run, so the spec and the published reference cannot drift apart. Hand-written prose is confined to `docs/concepts/`, which covers the things a spec cannot express — what a trip actually models, why pagination is cursor-based, which fields are stable enough to build on. The split follows from where each kind of content rots: endpoint shapes change constantly and mechanically, concepts change rarely and require judgement. Trying to hand-maintain the mechanical half produced a reference that was wrong in small ways all the time, which taught integrators to distrust the accurate half too.

Build artifacts land in `s3://halyard-build-artifacts` under three prefixes with different lifecycle rules: `pr/` expires after 10 days, `main/` after 60, and `releases/` never expires. The bucket had grown past four terabytes, almost entirely test binaries and coverage bundles from pull requests that closed months earlier, and the storage line had become visible enough that people were arguing about it in the wrong meeting. Release artifacts are exempt on purpose — they are the rollback path, and an expired release artifact turns a two-minute redeploy into a rebuild from an old tag whose toolchain may no longer resolve. The lifecycle rules live in `infra/storage/artifacts.tf`, and the publishing job picks the prefix from the ref so nothing depends on a human remembering which one to use. We also added a bucket size alarm at 6 TB, so the next growth surprise shows up as an alert rather than as an invoice.

House position, worth restating because every new integration asks: delivery is at-least-once, and every consumer must be safe to run twice. We do not chase exactly-once semantics, because the versions available to us are either broker features that only hold inside one broker's own world, or a distributed transaction we would then have to operate at three in the morning. The cheaper discipline is to make the effect idempotent — a unique constraint, an upsert keyed on the vendor's identifier, a conditional write guarded by a version — and then stop thinking about duplicates entirely. In review, the question we expect someone to ask of any new consumer is what happens when this message arrives a second time, and "it won't" is not an accepted answer. The corollary is that side effects which genuinely cannot be made idempotent, like sending a customer an email, need an explicit dedupe record written before the effect, and that record has to live somewhere durable rather than somewhere that may quietly evict it.

When something downstream is slow, the right response is to stop accepting work, not to grow a buffer in front of it. Unbounded in-memory queues inside a service turn a slow dependency into an out-of-memory kill, and the kill loses everything buffered, which is strictly worse than never having accepted the work in the first place — at least the broker still had it. This came up when someone proposed an internal queue in the notification service to smooth over carrier slowness. The answer was to lower the consumer's concurrency instead, so unprocessed work stays in the broker where it is durable, visible on a dashboard, and a capacity problem you can watch rather than an invisible one inside a process. The principle we keep landing on: the only buffer allowed to be large is the one that is durable and observable.

Every script under `scripts/` starts with `#!/usr/bin/env bash` and `set -euo pipefail`, and shellcheck runs over them in the fast hook set. The env-based shebang instead of `/bin/bash` is not stylistic: macOS still ships bash 3.2 at that path for licensing reasons, and our scripts use associative arrays and other bash 4+ features, so a hardcoded path produces a syntax error on a Mac while working fine everywhere else. The strict-mode line went in after a setup script continued past a failed step, left a half-configured environment behind, and then failed much later with a completely unrelated message; the person debugging it lost most of an afternoon. We do not write POSIX sh for these. The portability we actually need is macOS plus two Linux distributions, all of which have a modern bash available, and the readability cost of avoiding arrays was not worth a portability we never exercise. Anything past roughly two hundred lines gets rewritten in Python instead, which has happened twice.

Extended the blameless norm to cover the tools and processes people were following, not just the people. We had gotten good at not blaming the engineer who ran the wrong command, and correspondingly bad at examining why the command was easy to run wrong — the analysis would stop at "human error, we'll add a confirmation prompt" and move on. The reframing is that a person following the documented procedure and getting a bad outcome is a finding about the procedure, and it should be written up with the same seriousness as a code defect. In practice this changed what our action items look like: fewer prompts and warnings, more removals of the dangerous capability from the path where it wasn't needed. It also made people more willing to say "I did the thing the runbook said and it broke," which was previously a socially awkward sentence because it implicitly criticizes whoever wrote the runbook. We say explicitly at the start of each review that the runbook is a suspect too. The most valuable outcome so far was a rewrite of the failover procedure after two separate people misread the same ambiguous step in the same direction.

The laptop package baseline is a `Brewfile` in the dotfiles source, applied with `brew bundle --file ~/.config/homebrew/Brewfile`. It is short on purpose — ripgrep, fd, jq, gh, tmux, direnv, mise, colima, the docker CLI, mkcert — and the bar for adding something is that at least two people would notice its absence. `brew bundle check --verbose` runs as part of the doctor target, so a missing package gets reported rather than discovered halfway through a task. Linux contributors get an equivalent package list in the onboarding doc, maintained by hand: writing a cross-distro installer for ten packages would cost more than it saves and would rot the first time a package name changed upstream. We deliberately do not use the Brewfile for language runtimes or for casks. Runtimes are mise's job, and desktop applications are a personal choice nobody wants a shared script reinstalling on them.

Go service images build with a registry-backed BuildKit cache: `--cache-to type=registry,ref=registry.halyard.internal/<service>:buildcache,mode=max` and the matching `--cache-from`. Inline cache stopped being sufficient once the Dockerfiles went multi-stage, because inline only carries metadata for the final stage and the expensive dependency layer in the builder stage was being recomputed on every run. With `mode=max` the intermediate layers are exported too, and a no-op rebuild of dispatch-api went from about four minutes to under one. The cache ref is per-service and split by branch family — the default branch writes cache, pull request builds only read it — so a broken branch cannot poison the cache everyone else pulls from. Cache tags are garbage collected by the registry policy at thirty days. Nothing depends on the cache existing: a cold build is slower, never different.

Cache keys carry a schema generation prefix — `v7:rate:{origin}:{dest}:{service}` — and the current value lives in a single constant in `services/common/cache/keys.py`. When the shape of a cached value changes, we bump the prefix in the same commit as the change. That retires the entire previous generation atomically at deploy time without touching the cache server, and the orphaned keys age out under LRU by themselves. What we used to do was a targeted delete script, which required knowing the exact key pattern, ran `SCAN` across a few million keys, and was wrong on the one occasion it mattered because a service had been writing a slightly different pattern than the script assumed. `FLUSHDB` is worse again: it takes out every unrelated cache at the same moment and hands origin a cold start it did not need. The mildly annoying part is that a bump costs one generation of memory for a few hours until eviction catches up, which is exactly why the cache cluster is sized with headroom instead of run at ninety-five percent.

We cache things that are slow or that cost us money at a third party, not things that are merely called often. A primary key lookup against the database, on a warm connection, returning a small row, is not meaningfully slower than a round trip to the cache plus deserialisation — and it is one source of truth instead of two. The reflex to cache everything came up again in the quote path review and the answer was the same as the last two times: show the latency profile first. Where caching earns its place it tends to be obvious, because the thing being avoided is a carrier API call measured in hundreds of milliseconds or a report query measured in seconds. The cost people consistently underweight is not memory or infrastructure spend, it is that every cached value becomes a second thing that can be wrong, and staleness bugs get reported by customers rather than caught by tests.

Split the versioning schemes deliberately: the tideboard web app uses calendar versioning as `YYYY.MM.patch`, while the Go libraries and the published client SDK stay on semver. The reasoning is entirely about audience. Nothing consumes tideboard as a dependency — it is a deployed app behind a login — so a major version bump communicated nothing beyond someone having an opinion about how large the change felt, and we watched two arguments about whether a redesign was major or minor before concluding the question was empty. The client SDK does have external consumers resolving version ranges, and there semver carries real information about breakage. The version in `package.json` is written by the release script from the tag; nobody edits it by hand, and the pre-tag check compares the two and refuses to proceed on a mismatch.

Pull request workflows set `concurrency: group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}` with `cancel-in-progress: true`, so pushing a fixup kills the run for the previous commit instead of queueing behind it. On busy afternoons that alone cut runner contention by roughly a third, and nobody has ever cared about the result of a superseded run. The release and publish workflows explicitly set `cancel-in-progress: false`. Cancelling a run halfway through pushing a multi-arch manifest leaves the registry with a partial index that later pulls resolve inconsistently, and untangling that by hand is an unpleasant twenty minutes at exactly the wrong moment. The asymmetry is intentional and there is a comment at the top of both release workflows saying so, because it looks like an oversight and someone will otherwise tidy it into consistency.

Outbound concurrency to each carrier is held at roughly sixty percent of the ceiling in the contract rather than at the ceiling. Two reasons. The published limit is per account, and our sandbox plus the load tests share that account, so running at the line means a test run pushes production over it. And being throttled by a carrier is not a clean fast failure — one of them responds by silently queueing our requests and answering minutes later, which looks exactly like an outage from inside our system and costs a support ticket plus most of a day with their integrations team to untangle. The margin is cheap: we are nowhere near being limited by carrier throughput at current volumes, and if we ever get there the correct move is renegotiating the contract, not shaving the buffer. Reviewed the numbers in the spring and left them where they were.

Carrier tracking callbacks are deduped in the database, not in application logic. `tracking_events` carries a unique index `uniq_carrier_event` on `(carrier_code, carrier_event_id)`, and the ingest path inserts with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, treating zero rows affected as a successful no-op. Every carrier we integrate with retries callbacks, and one of them retries aggressively enough that we routinely see the same event four or five times inside a second. The in-memory dedupe we had before only worked when both copies happened to land on the same pod, which is to say it worked in testing and not in production. Doing it at the database means the guarantee does not depend on which replica answers, on the cache being up, or on how many pods are running. The cost is one extra index and a little write amplification, which is nothing against the class of bug it removes. This is now the default pattern for anything consuming an external event stream: find the vendor's event identifier, put a unique constraint on it, and let the database be the dedupe store.

Each service repo keeps a hand-written `CHANGELOG.md` at its root with an `## Unreleased` heading at the top. The entry is written in the same PR as the change it describes, by the person who made the change, and reviewers treat a missing entry the same as a missing test for anything user-visible. Cutting a release just renames the `## Unreleased` heading to the version and adds a fresh empty one. We tried generating the file from commit history and it failed for the obvious reason: commit subjects are written for engineers reading a diff, and the changelog is read by support and by the console team, who do not know what the fan-out stage is. Writing the line at the moment of the change also forces the author to answer whether anyone outside the repo would notice at all, which is a cheap sanity check on scope. Internal-only refactors get no entry, deliberately, so the file stays short enough that people read it.

Release notes are generated from commit trailers rather than written from memory. Every commit reaching the default branch must carry a `Change-Type:` trailer with one of `feature`, `fix`, `chore` or `breaking`, and `scripts/changelog.py` groups them under the tag being cut. The `changelog-lint` job fails a pull request whose commits lack the trailer, which is irritating exactly once per new joiner and then becomes muscle memory. Hand-written notes drifted from reality within about two releases: someone would fix something on Wednesday, the notes had been drafted Tuesday, and the customer-visible changelog quietly became fiction that support then had to correct. Generating from trailers means the notes cannot describe more or less than what actually shipped. It does not solve wording — the release owner still edits the generated file before the tag is annotated, and that edit goes through review like any other change.

Dotfiles are managed with chezmoi, source of truth at `~/.local/share/chezmoi`, applied with `chezmoi apply` and reviewed with `chezmoi diff` first — the diff step is spelled out in the onboarding doc because applying dotfiles blind is how people lose local edits. The previous scheme was a bare git repo with symlinks, and it broke the first time someone set up a Fedora laptop: config paths differed, a branch per OS appeared, and the branches had diverged within a month. Templating turned the OS difference into an explicit conditional in one file instead of a fork. Machine-specific values — hostname, work versus personal identity, whether the container runtime is installed — come from template data prompted at first init rather than from hand-edited files, so re-applying stays idempotent. Each engineer's repo is their own; what is shared is the tooling config we consider baseline, pulled in as a chezmoi external from a small internal repo, so an update to the shared shell functions reaches everyone on their next apply without touching anything personal.

Narrowed the CI runner's cloud role after the December access review found it could read every bucket in the account, not just build artifacts. The role was created back when Halyard had one pipeline and nobody bothered to revisit it as we grew to eleven. Replaced the wildcard resource with an explicit prefix list and added a condition key so the role only assumes from our own runner pool. Verified nothing broke by running the full pipeline against the new policy in a shadow account for four days before cutting over. Two jobs did break: the release notes generator was reading a bucket it had no business reading, and the docs publisher wrote to a path outside its prefix. Both were fixed rather than granted an exception, which was the whole point of doing this. The policy now lives at `infra/iam/ci_runner_policy.json` and is generated from a template so the prefix list stays in sync with the pipeline definitions. Rule going forward: any new bucket a CI job needs gets added to that template with a one-line justification comment, and the review happens in the same PR as the job change. No out-of-band grants.

Moved the laptop container runtime from Docker Desktop to Colima in January 2026, after the seat licence renewal came in at a number nobody wanted to defend. Colima starts as `colima start --cpu 4 --memory 8 --disk 60 --vm-type vz --mount-type virtiofs`, and bootstrap writes those into `~/.colima/default/colima.yaml` so nobody has to remember the flags. The vz and virtiofs combination mattered far more than the CPU allocation: under the older sshfs mount the API test suite spent most of its wall time on file stats, and the switch took a cold `make test` from just over four minutes to about ninety seconds on an M2. The docker CLI still comes from Homebrew and the socket path is exported in the shell rc, so compose files and tooling needed no changes at all. Two engineers stayed on Docker Desktop with personal licences and that is fine — nothing in any repo assumes Colima specifically, only that a Docker-compatible socket exists at the exported path.

Code comments here answer why, and where the reason is a decision rather than a local fact, the comment cites it instead of restating it — `# see ADR 0031` next to the constant, not a paragraph paraphrasing the ADR badly. Paraphrases were the problem: they were written once, never updated when the decision was superseded, and read as authoritative. A pointer at least fails honestly, since a missing ADR number is obvious. Reviewers are expected to ask for a comment whenever a diff introduces a magic number, an ordering constraint, or a workaround for something outside the repo, and to leave everything else alone. Nobody is asked to comment a function that says what its name says.

Commit subjects are imperative, under 72 characters, and prefixed with the component: `ingest: drop duplicate pings before fan-out`. The body, when there is one, answers why rather than what — the diff already covers what. The working test is that `git log --oneline` over a release range should read as a plausible first draft of release notes to someone on another team. We do not enforce a machine-parseable commit convention and have declined it twice; nothing downstream consumes the commit type, so the only thing a strict grammar would buy is a lint failure on the last commit of a long day. The one trailer we do care about is `Co-authored-by` on pair work, because attribution is the kind of thing that is annoying to reconstruct later and free to record at the time.

Rewrote the event pipeline backlog alert to threshold on estimated drain time rather than raw message count. The old rule was `fleet_events_consumer_lag > 5000 for 10m`, which fired constantly during the morning surge when consumers were healthily working through a burst, and stayed silent one afternoon when a single partition was stuck at 900 messages and had not moved in an hour. Message count says nothing about whether you are falling behind.

The replacement divides lag by the consumer's processed-rate over the last five minutes, giving a projected seconds-to-drain, and pages when that exceeds 900 for ten minutes. A companion rule catches the divide-by-zero case that the first version missed: if lag is above zero and the processed rate is exactly zero for five minutes, that is a stuck consumer and pages immediately, because the projection is infinite and the original expression evaluated to NaN and silently never fired. That NaN gap cost us forty minutes on the stuck-partition incident and is the reason the rule file has a comment on that line.

When the cache is unreachable, read paths fall through to origin and eat the latency rather than failing the request. This is not free — during the April failover the read replica saw about nine times its normal rate and got uncomfortably warm — but a slow shipment lookup is a bad minute for a customer while a failed one is a support ticket. We took that risk knowingly, and it is why the replica is sized with more headroom than its steady-state load would suggest. The important exception is anything where the cache is the source of truth rather than a copy: dedupe records and locks. Those fail closed, because falling through to "no record found" means doing the thing twice, and a duplicate label or a duplicate customer notification is worse than an error page. So the rule has two halves — copies degrade, state does not — and which half a new cache read falls into is a review question every single time.

Standardised the default time range on service dashboards to the last six hours. It used to be twenty-four, inherited from whoever built the first board, and during incidents that was actively harmful: a five-minute outage is a hairline on a day-wide axis, and people were zooming in as their first action every single time, then forgetting to zoom back out and misreading a stale window later.

Six hours is long enough to see the shape of the current day — the morning dispatch surge, the afternoon plateau — and short enough that a short outage is visibly a cliff. Anything requiring longer context gets a purpose-built board rather than a wider default; the capacity and seasonality boards open on thirty days and are explicitly labelled as trend views so nobody mistakes one for a live view during an incident.

The supporting habit is that every incident-facing board carries a week-over-week comparison row at the bottom, so the trend question can be answered without changing the range at the top. That turned out to matter more than the default itself.

Dashboards live in `observability/dashboards/` as jsonnet and are provisioned into Grafana read-only; the UI editor is for exploration, not for saving. Before this, the source of truth was whatever the last person clicked, and we lost the main dispatch board twice — once to an accidental overwrite, once to a folder permission change nobody could explain. Now `make dashboards-build` renders JSON into `build/dashboards/` and CI fails if the rendered output differs from what the provisioner would deploy, which also gives reviewers a readable diff of query changes rather than a four-thousand-line JSON blob.

The shared library holds the row templates — a RED row, a saturation row, a dependency row — so a new service dashboard is about thirty lines and looks like every other one. That consistency is worth more than the version control, honestly: during an incident nobody hunts for where the error-rate panel is hiding, because it is always top-left. Exploration still happens in the UI, and the workflow for keeping something is to export the panel JSON and paste it into a jsonnet block, which is clunky enough that people only do it for panels they genuinely intend to keep.

Deleted the host and container CPU utilization alerts entirely. Over eighteen months of incident records, not one customer-visible outage was first detected by them, and they accounted for roughly a third of all after-hours notifications. High CPU on the route planner is normal — it is a solver, it is supposed to saturate a core while it works. Low CPU during a real outage is also common, because a wedged service is doing nothing at all.

What we kept is saturation signals with a direct line to user pain: run queue depth relative to allocated cores, and memory working set against the limit, because that one ends in an out-of-memory kill rather than mere slowness. Both of those are ticket severity, not page severity.

The general lesson we wrote down at the time is that a resource metric is only alertable if you can finish the sentence "and therefore a customer experiences...". CPU never finishes that sentence on its own. It remains extremely useful as the second thing you look at once a symptom alert has told you where to look, and it is still on every service dashboard.

Moved the vulnerability scanner off the per-PR path and onto a weekly scheduled job. Running it on every pull request meant a new CVE published on Tuesday would fail unrelated PRs on Wednesday, and people learned to re-run CI until it passed or to merge with the check red. Both are worse than not running it. The weekly job now opens a single tracking issue with the full delta since the last run, assigned to whoever is on the platform rotation that week. That person triages: real exposure gets a fix, transitive-only-in-a-dev-dependency gets a note and a suppression with an expiry date. The scheduled workflow is `.github/workflows/dep_audit.yml` and it writes its output to the issue body rather than only to the job log, because nobody reads job logs for scheduled jobs. Suppressions live in `audit-suppressions.toml` with a mandatory `expires` field; the job fails loudly if a suppression is past its date, which is the one failure mode we do want to be noisy. This trades immediacy for actually being read, and after two quarters the triage backlog is consistently under five items.

Split the automated dependency update bot into two streams because one stream was training everyone to rubber-stamp. Patch and minor updates to dependencies we consider low-risk now batch into a single weekly PR that CI must pass and that one person approves without line-by-line review. Major versions, anything in the crypto or serialization families, and anything that touches the request path get individual PRs with a required review from someone who knows that area. The classification lives in `deps/risk_tiers.yaml` with a default of high, so an unclassified new dependency lands in the careful stream until somebody deliberately downgrades it. Before this, thirty small PRs a week meant nobody looked at any of them, including the one that bumped a template engine across a major version and changed autoescaping defaults. That one shipped and we found it in staging, which was luck. Batching the boring ones bought back the attention to actually read the interesting ones. The weekly batch takes about ten minutes to review; the individual PRs take as long as they take, and that asymmetry is the entire point of the design.

Work expected to run longer than two weeks, or which changes an interface another team depends on, gets a short design document before implementation starts. Everything under that bar is designed in the pull request description, and that counts as complete. Both halves of the rule are load-bearing. We went through a stretch where design docs were written for almost everything, largely as a signal of seriousness, and they were long, unread, and mostly a transcription of a decision already made — which taught people that documents are theatre. Restricting the practice to work that is genuinely expensive to get wrong made the remaining documents short, actually contested in review, and worth reading later. The two-week figure is arbitrary and nobody argues about borderline cases; the cross-team clause is the one that gets invoked in practice, because that is where the cost of a bad interface lands on people who had no say in it.

Evaluated fully containerised development environments in late 2025 and declined them, at least for now. The pitch was legitimate — one definition of the environment, no drift between laptops, new hires productive in a single command — and the trial was a genuine two-week spike on the API repo rather than a hallway opinion. What killed it was the everyday experience. File watching through the container mount was slow enough that the reload loop went from imperceptible to roughly four seconds, the debugger integration needed per-editor configuration nobody was going to maintain across three editors, and the image itself became a thing to keep current, which is the same maintenance we were trying to escape, relocated rather than removed. The setup time it would have saved was about two hours per new engineer a handful of times a year, and we already spend more than that maintaining the toolchain we have. Writing this down so it gets re-litigated with evidence rather than from scratch: revisit if onboarding setup starts exceeding half a day, or if we grow a second team that does not share the current toolchain.

Wrote `bin/dlq_replay` so requeuing dead letters is a reviewed operation instead of a shell one-liner someone improvises at 2am. Usage is `bin/dlq_replay --queue tracking.ingest --since 2h`, which defaults to a dry run and prints a histogram of messages by original exception class and age. Actually publishing requires `--yes`, and the tool refuses to run when the target queue has zero consumers, because replaying into a queue nobody is reading just moves the pile sideways. It stamps a `x-replayed-at` header, so a message that dead-letters a second time is visible as a repeat instead of looking fresh. The ceremony exists because of the March fan-out incident: someone replayed roughly forty thousand messages into a queue whose consumers were still failing, which re-dead-lettered all of them with new timestamps and destroyed our ability to separate original failures from replays. The order encoded in the tool's help text is fix the consumer, deploy it, watch the queue drain, then replay.

`handbook/glossary.md` is the single canonical definition of our domain terms — `trip`, `leg`, `ping`, `dwell`, `assignment` — and code, tracker issues and customer-facing copy are all expected to use the glossary spelling and meaning. The forcing incident was `leg`: the ingest side used it for a segment between two stops, the insights side used it for a driver-shift boundary, and a report shipped that silently mixed the two for six weeks. Nobody had lied; the two teams had never spoken the word in the same room. Adding a term is a PR against the handbook with a one-paragraph definition and, where it helps, an explicit "not to be confused with" line. Renaming a term is a much bigger deal and needs an ADR in the affected service, because identifiers, database columns and customer documentation all follow the glossary.

Removed the build status badge from the top of the service READMEs. It only ever reflected the most recent run on the default branch, but people read it as a health indicator for the running system, and twice during incidents someone cited a green badge as evidence that things were fine. A badge that answers a question nobody is asking, sitting in a place where it gets mistaken for the answer to a question people are asking, is worse than no badge at all. The dashboards answer the health question properly and the pipeline history answers the build question properly, and neither of those lives in a README. Nobody has asked for it back in the eight months since.

Removed the hierarchical federation setup where a central Prometheus scraped `/federate` on each cluster's local Prometheus. It was failing silently at the worst possible moments: a federate scrape pulling tens of thousands of series took longer than the scrape timeout under load, the request was cut off, and the central store recorded a gap. The gaps correlated with incidents, because incidents are when load is high — so the global view lost data exactly when someone was looking at it.

Each cluster Prometheus now ships to the central store with a `remote_write` block in its config, with the queue tuned upward from the defaults after the first attempt hit shard limits during the morning surge and buffered to disk. Remote write applies backpressure and retries rather than losing a window, and the delivery lag is visible as a metric we alert on, which the federation setup never exposed.

The migration ran both paths in parallel for two weeks and compared a handful of key series between them, which is how we discovered the gaps had been happening for far longer than anyone realised — roughly weekly, not the once or twice we had noticed.

We support a floor, not an editor. The floor is that whatever you use respects the shared whitespace config, runs the project formatter on save, and talks to the language servers we configure; beyond that the choice is yours and we will happily help you set it up. Standardising on a single editor comes up roughly once a year, usually framed as making pairing and onboarding easier, and we have declined it every time. Two of the strongest engineers here have deeply customised terminal setups built over a decade, and the productivity they would lose is immediate and real, whereas the consistency benefit is speculative and mostly accrues to whoever is making the argument. What we invested in instead was making the shared configuration easy to copy from, and making sure nothing in the build, test or debug path assumes a particular editor. When someone new arrives with no strong preference we point them at what most of the team uses, because a setup other people can help you fix beats a marginally better one you maintain alone.

`.editorconfig` at each repo root is the single cross-editor source of truth for whitespace, and it is deliberately boring: `root = true`, `end_of_line = lf`, `insert_final_newline = true`, `trim_trailing_whitespace = true`, four spaces for Python, two for TypeScript, JSON and YAML, tabs for Makefiles. It exists because a contractor working on Windows sent two pull requests whose diffs were almost entirely CRLF churn with about nine real changed lines buried inside, and reviewing those cost more than the feature did. The formatters would have caught most of it eventually, but editorconfig catches it at the keystroke rather than at the commit, and it works in the editors we do not configure centrally. Nothing else about style belongs in that file — indentation and line endings only. Line length, quote style and import order belong to the formatter, and duplicating them here just created two places that could disagree.

Every repo carries a committed `.envrc` whose entire job is to call `use mise` and export the handful of local-only variables the dev stack needs: database URL, log level, the local API base URL. Anything machine-specific goes in `.envrc.local`, which is gitignored and sourced at the end if present, so nobody edits the committed file and then has to remember not to commit it. Real credentials live in neither file; the two services that need them read from a thin wrapper around the vault CLI at process start, so the secret exists in the process and not on disk. We kept direnv's manual allow step rather than auto-approving. It looks like pure friction on every branch switch that touches `.envrc`, and people have asked to disable it twice, but an `.envrc` is executable shell that arrives with a checkout, and typing `direnv allow` after reading a two-line diff is a cheap habit to keep. The bootstrap target adds the `eval "$(direnv hook zsh)"` line and then prints a reminder to open a new shell, because the most common first-day support question was "why are my env vars empty" and the answer was always that the hook had not loaded yet.

Every alert rule carries a `runbook_url` annotation resolving to `runbooks/<alert_name>.md` in the same repo as the rule, and `make lint-alerts` fails the build for any rule missing it. The runbook's first line must be one sentence saying what the alert actually means in terms of customer impact — not what the query measures, which the rule already states. That first sentence is the entire value of the file at three in the morning; everything after it is a bonus. Runbooks are allowed to be short and are allowed to say "nobody knows yet, ask in the ingest channel", which is honest and still better than a dead link. Keeping the runbook next to the rule, rather than in the handbook, means the two move in the same PR when a threshold changes, and we stopped seeing runbooks that described a threshold retired two quarters earlier.

Agreed that a dashboard without a named owning team is a liability, not an asset, and gets archived. We had drifted to something like sixty dashboards, most built during one incident and never touched again. The harm is not clutter, it is that during the next incident somebody opens a plausible-looking board, reads a panel whose query has silently returned nothing since a metric was renamed, and concludes the wrong thing with confidence. An empty panel reads as "no problem here" to a stressed person.

So the rule is: the owning team goes in the dashboard description, and anything unowned at the quarterly sweep moves to an archive folder rather than being deleted, since the archive has rescued two boards nobody would have rebuilt from scratch. Ownership means someone is accountable for the panels still returning data, not for the board being pretty. The side effect we did not predict was healthy — several teams chose to let their boards be archived rather than claim them, which told us more about what people actually use during an incident than any survey would have.

Turned on exemplar storage so a spike on a latency panel is one click from a trace of a request that caused it. Prometheus runs with `--enable-feature=exemplar-storage`, the Go services attach the trace ID to histogram observations, and the Grafana data source has the trace-to-logs style link configured to open the trace backend by ID.

The motivation was pure incident ergonomics. The old loop was: notice p99 spike, guess a time window, go to the trace search UI, filter by service and duration, hope a slow trace was sampled in that window. That is five steps and two chances to lose the thread, and it usually failed because head sampling had discarded the interesting one. Now the exemplar is a dot on the graph that is guaranteed to be retained, because the tail sampler keeps anything over a second anyway.

Exemplars are stored in a fixed-size circular buffer, so they are not durable — anything older than a couple of hours has aged out. This surprised someone reviewing an incident two days later. For retrospective work the trace IDs need to be copied out while the incident is live, which is now a line in the incident template.

Every new engineer is paired with a buddy on their team for their first two cycles, and their first merged change is expected to be a documentation fix they found while following the setup instructions. This is not busywork and it is not a hazing ritual — it is the only reliable way we have found to detect documentation decay, because a newcomer is the single person in the building who reads the setup guide literally rather than from memory. It also gets them through the full change pipeline on something with no risk attached, so the first time they use the review and release path is not the day they are shipping something that matters. The buddy's job is explicitly to be interruptible, not to assign work; the team lead still assigns work, and conflating the two produced buddies who felt like reluctant managers.

Agreed rules for quarantining a flaky test: anyone whose build it blocked may quarantine it immediately, without asking permission, but the same commit must name an owner and the quarantine carries a two week clock. If it has not been fixed or deliberately deleted by then it gets deleted, and that deletion needs no further debate. The clock is the entire point of the agreement. Quarantine used to be a graveyard — we had tests parked for over a year, nobody remembered what behaviour they were meant to protect, and their continued presence created a sense of coverage that was worse than the honest absence would have been. The other half of the agreement is that quarantining is not a mark against whoever wrote the test. A flake is usually a design signal about hidden timing or shared state rather than carelessness, and treating it as a personal failure only meant people suffered the flake in silence and re-ran the job instead of flagging it.

We run worker counts roughly flat through the day instead of scaling reactively on queue depth. Every new pod costs a burst of broker connections, a cold local cache, and a carrier authentication round trip before it does a single unit of useful work, so the first thirty seconds of a scale-up actively makes the backlog worse — which then triggers more scale-up. Scaling in is worse still: the drain window has to cover the longest-running job, so the pods you are trying to remove linger long enough that the autoscaler's next decision gets made on stale information. Flat capacity, sized for the busy part of the day, is boring and predictable and cheap enough that the finance conversation has never once come up. Where load is genuinely and predictably different — Monday morning, and the two days before a major retail holiday — we raise the floor on a schedule, which is a decision a human made in advance rather than a control loop guessing under pressure.

We ended the formatting debate by agreeing that the formatter's output is the style guide, full stop. Nobody argues about line length, quote style or import order any more, and the rule we wrote down is that a review comment about whitespace or formatting is out of order: if the formatter accepted it, it is fine, and if you disagree with the formatter you open a discussion about the formatter configuration, not about someone's pull request. The rationale is that the real cost of a style disagreement is never the style. It is the extra round trip and the low-grade friction of being corrected on something arbitrary, and nobody has ever managed to show that one convention made code more readable in a way that survived a week of familiarity. The one thing we negotiated carefully was the initial configuration, because that change touched every file and had to land once, deliberately, on a quiet afternoon with everyone's branches merged or rebased the same day. Since then the config has changed twice in eighteen months, both times to relax something that was generating noise rather than to tighten anything.

Global git settings ship as an include rather than a whole file. `~/.config/git/config` stays personal — user.email, the signing key reference, personal aliases — and ends with an include of `~/.config/git/larkspur.inc`, which chezmoi manages. The shared include sets `rerere.enabled = true`, `fetch.prune = true`, `pull.rebase = true`, `diff.algorithm = histogram` and `init.defaultBranch = main`. The indirection exists because the first version of the dotfiles wrote a complete gitconfig and cheerfully overwrote two people's commit identity and one person's signing setup; splitting personal from shared made applying dotfiles stop being a scary operation. rerere is the setting people actually notice: on a branch rebased repeatedly onto a moving main, resolving the same conflict once instead of five times is worth the occasional surprise, and the surprise is documented in the onboarding notes. `diff.algorithm = histogram` went in after a refactor produced a diff that interleaved two functions and made the review pointless.

Internal gRPC clients set `grpc.keepalive_time_ms = 20000` and `grpc.keepalive_timeout_ms = 5000`, with keepalive permitted without an active stream. The internal load balancer in front of `rating-engine` idles TCP flows out at 350 seconds and does it silently — no reset — so the first call from `shipment-api` after a quiet stretch would hang until the deadline and surface as UNAVAILABLE. Overnight, and on the low-traffic regional deployment all day, this reliably meant the first request of the morning failed, which is the worst possible thing to be flaky since it is exactly what a synthetic check hits. Twenty seconds sits comfortably under the idle timer and costs nothing: the frames are tiny and there are only a few dozen client pods. The server side had to be configured to tolerate that rate, because a mismatched minimum ping interval makes the server send GOAWAY and leaves you worse off than before. Check both halves when adding a new internal service.

Every markdown file under `handbook/` carries front matter with two keys: `owner: team-ingest` and `reviewed: 2026-05-02`. The owner is always a team, never a person, because people change teams and a personal owner quietly becomes no owner. Documents whose owning team has been dissolved get moved to `handbook/attic/` with the front matter intact rather than deleted — the attic is excluded from search ranking but still greppable, which turned out to matter twice during audits when someone needed to prove what the policy had been in a given quarter. The `reviewed` date is only bumped when a human actually reread the document; bumping it as part of an unrelated edit is treated as a small dishonesty, because the whole staleness sweep depends on that field meaning what it claims.

Anyone can push directly to `handbook/` — typo fixes, clarifications, adding a page — with no review at all. The exception is `handbook/policy/`, which is guarded by CODEOWNERS and needs approval from two leads before merge. This asymmetry was the fix for a handbook that had gone read-only in practice: when everything needed review, small corrections were not worth the ceremony, so people stopped making them and the pages slowly diverged from reality.
