Making the cheap edits free restored the flow of small fixes, and confining review to the fifteen or so pages that describe how we treat each other keeps the guardrail where it actually matters. Every direct push shows up in the handbook channel feed, so open does not mean unobserved; twice a change has been reverted by discussion the same day, which is exactly the intended failure mode.

Rewrote the latency histogram buckets for `dispatch_api_request_duration_seconds` so a bucket boundary lands exactly on every SLO threshold we quote. The old buckets were the client library defaults, which put edges at 0.1 and 0.25 while our interactive target is 300 ms — meaning the p99 estimate was linearly interpolated across a bucket four times wider than the thing we were measuring, and the reported quantile could swing sixty milliseconds with no change in real traffic. New boundaries are 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10. The 0.3 boundary is the load-bearing one: the SLO burn rate rule now reads a bucket count directly instead of a quantile, which is exact rather than estimated, and the panel showing "fraction of requests under 300 ms" is computed from the same series the alert uses. Two extra buckets per label set cost us roughly 4 percent more series on that metric, which was acceptable given we had already dropped the per-device labels. The same boundary discipline was applied to `route_planner_solve_duration_seconds`, where the target is 4 s and the bucket set is much coarser.

We pulled the type check and the unit test run out of the commit hooks, and the reasoning is worth keeping because the instinct is always to add more. The thorough hook set was correct in the sense that it caught real problems before they were pushed, and useless in practice because it took long enough that people learned the flag that skips hooks — and once someone habitually skips hooks, they skip all of them, including the ten-millisecond one that catches a stray debug print. A fast hook everybody runs is worth more than a thorough one half the team bypasses. So the commit hook now does only things that are near-instant and mechanically fixable, and the slower, more valuable checks moved to where waiting is expected and nobody is blocked at the keyboard. The corollary we keep restating whenever someone proposes an addition: if a check is slow, the answer is to make it faster or to move it later, not to accept a slow hook because the check matters.

Container images are pushed as `registry.halyard.internal/<service>:<git-sha>` and that sha tag is the canonical one. The moving `:main` tag exists only for humans poking around by hand and is never referenced by a deployment manifest. Release builds additionally get a version tag, `dispatch-api:v2.14.0` for instance, applied to the identical digest rather than produced by a second build. The rule came from an afternoon where a rollout half-completed against `:main` while a new push landed, and we ended up with two pods running genuinely different code and a bug that only reproduced on one of them. Referencing an immutable sha tag makes the fleet's state legible from the manifest alone, which is worth the slightly uglier YAML. `scripts/publish-image.sh` is the only sanctioned path to push, and it refuses to run against a dirty working tree, because the sha in the tag would then be a lie about the contents of the image.

Put a small in-process cache in front of Redis for the carrier service catalogue: `cachetools.TTLCache(maxsize=2048, ttl=30)`, lock-guarded, in the rating path. The catalogue changes maybe twice a month but is read on every quote, and at peak we were doing forty thousand Redis GETs a second for about three hundred distinct values. Thirty seconds of staleness is acceptable specifically here, because a service code that disappears mid-window fails at the carrier anyway and that error path already exists. The two-tier arrangement is not the default and should not spread. It makes invalidation genuinely harder — bumping the Redis key does nothing until every pod's local copy expires on its own schedule — and it introduces a window where two pods disagree. We only reach for it where the value set is small, the read rate is extreme, and staleness is provably harmless. Anyone proposing this pattern for a new caller has to answer what breaks when one pod is thirty seconds behind another.

Split the communications role out from the incident commander after a bad night where the person coordinating the technical response was also fielding questions from three different internal channels and drafting a status page update. Predictably, all three suffered. The comms owner now handles every outbound message — status page, internal updates, the executive summary — and explicitly shields the commander from anyone asking for an ETA. The commander's only external obligation is a two-sentence state update to the comms owner every fifteen minutes, which is short enough to give while thinking about something else. What surprised us is that the comms owner does not need to be technical. The two best ones we've had came from support, because they already knew how to describe a problem in terms a customer cares about and they were not tempted to dive into the debugging. We also learned to fill this role early rather than waiting to see if an incident gets big enough to need it. Filling it late means the first twenty minutes of communication were already handled badly, and the first twenty minutes are the ones people remember.

Redefined our severity levels around user-visible impact rather than around which system is broken. The old rubric was written in terms of components — a database issue was automatically high severity, a frontend issue automatically lower — which produced a steady stream of misclassified incidents. A read replica falling over at three in the morning with zero user impact was waking people up, while a broken checkout flow that only affected one region was being triaged as routine. The new definitions are phrased entirely as what a customer would experience: cannot complete a core action, degraded but usable, cosmetic or internal only. Nobody argues about which component is involved anymore because the component doesn't enter into it. The secondary benefit we didn't anticipate: the severity now maps cleanly onto what we tell customers, so the status page update writes itself from the incident record instead of being composed from scratch under pressure. The pushback was from the infrastructure side, who felt this undervalued near-misses on critical systems. We addressed that separately with a near-miss log that carries no paging obligation but does get reviewed monthly.

Incident write-ups go in `docs/incidents/` named `YYYY-MM-DD-slug.md`, for example `docs/incidents/2026-03-11-ingest-lag.md`, and always in the repo of the service that was degraded rather than in a central pile. The skeleton has four sections: impact in customer-visible terms, timeline, contributing factors, and what changed. Two conventions matter. Timeline entries are pasted from the channel with UTC `HH:MM` prefixes and are not tidied up afterwards — the messy version preserves what was believed at the time, which is the only part later readers cannot reconstruct. And the third section is deliberately plural: contributing factors, never root cause. The single-cause framing kept producing write-ups that stopped at the last change merged before the alert fired, which is where the search ends rather than where the story starts. A write-up is expected within a week; a thin one filed on time is worth more than a thorough one that never lands, and several of ours are three paragraphs.

Stood up a module proxy and set `GOPROXY = https://proxy.halyard.internal,direct` in both the CI environment and the dev shell, after an upstream outage stalled a release cut for four hours with nothing to point at but a network error. The proxy caches every module version we have ever resolved, so a build that succeeded once can be rebuilt even if the origin disappears — which matters most for tagged releases we are contractually able to reproduce. Checksum verification is unchanged; the proxy serves what the sum database already attests, it does not become a trust root, and we were careful to say that out loud when the change was reviewed because it looks like the kind of thing that quietly weakens verification. Second-order benefit we did not plan for: the proxy access log is the cheapest inventory we have of what the services actually import, and it answered a customer security questionnaire in an afternoon that would otherwise have been days of grepping lock files.

Rolled out mutual TLS between internal services, replacing the previous model where anything inside the network could call anything else and services identified callers by a header the caller set about itself. That header was trusted, which is to say it was not a security control at all, and one service had a bug where it forwarded the header from an inbound public request. Certificates are issued per-service-identity with a short lifetime and rotated automatically by the sidecar; the identity is derived from the workload's service account rather than from anything the workload asserts. Rollout was permissive-mode first for six weeks, logging every connection that would have been rejected, which found eleven callers we did not know existed, including a long-forgotten reporting script running on someone's desktop. Enforcement went service by service starting with the ones handling payment data. The remaining permissive holdout is the metrics scrape path, which we've deliberately left because tightening it would require replacing the collector and the exposure is limited to read-only telemetry. That decision is recorded so the next person to notice it doesn't spend a day working out whether it's an oversight. It isn't.

Each team nominates one engineer per cycle as the shield: they take inbound questions from other teams, triage anything filed as `kind/interrupt`, and are the default answer to "who do I ask about ingest this week". The rotation lives in `handbook/rituals/shield.md`. The shield's committed work for that cycle is planned at roughly half the usual load, and planning treats that as a real cost rather than a fiction to be quietly overrun — the first two cycles we did not halve it and the shield simply worked longer days. This is a separate concern from the paging rotation and the two are deliberately never merged; the shield covers daylight-hours attention, not production response. The second-order benefit surprised us: having a named person made other teams stop DMing whoever they happened to know, which had been concentrating interruptions on the three longest-tenured engineers.

The cycle kickoff brief circulates the working day before the meeting, and the meeting itself exists only to resolve disagreements recorded as comments on the brief. Items that drew no comment are considered agreed and are not read aloud, which routinely turns a scheduled hour into eighteen minutes. The change came from noticing that the old kickoff spent most of its time transmitting information that was already written down, to an audience that had already read it, in the one hour of the day when every timezone was awake — the single scarcest resource the team has. Reserving synchronous time for genuine ambiguity is the whole principle, and it generalises: if a meeting's agenda can be satisfied by reading, it should have been a document. The obligation this creates is real and falls on the person writing the brief, who now has to make it good enough to be agreed with in silence. That is a fair trade, since one person writing carefully costs less than nine people listening.

`label-render` tasks run four to forty seconds because they block on carrier PDF endpoints. With Celery's default prefetch, the first worker to start grabbed a large slice of the queue and held it while later pods sat idle, so p95 label latency was decided by queue position rather than carrier speed. Set `worker_prefetch_multiplier = 1` and `task_acks_late = True` for that worker's config only. Now a pod holds exactly one job, a pod that dies returns its job to the broker instead of losing it, and adding capacity actually drains the backlog. Deliberately left the defaults alone on `notify-worker`, where tasks are around twenty milliseconds and one-at-a-time fetching would make the broker round trip the dominant cost. The general shape worth remembering: prefetch is a bet that your tasks are short and uniform. Long, variable tasks want a prefetch of one; short uniform ones want a fat prefetch. If a single queue contains both, that is usually a sign it should be two queues with two worker deployments.

Settled the argument about which latency statistic goes in an SLO: every latency target here is stated as a high percentile, never a mean or median. The reason is concrete. Mean dispatch latency looked healthy all through the winter complaints, because the slow calls were roughly one in two hundred and the fast majority buried them; drivers were retrying because their handset spun for eight seconds, and the graph showed two hundred milliseconds. A percentile makes the tail the subject of the sentence, which is the point — the tail is what a human notices.

We deliberately stopped at the ninety-ninth and refused the argument for a higher one. On the lower-traffic endpoints a five-minute window holds only a few hundred requests, so a nine-nines figure is dominated by two or three samples and the alert becomes a coin flip. Where someone genuinely needs to see the extreme tail, the answer is the max bucket plus traces, not a finer quantile in the SLO document. Means still appear on capacity dashboards, where they are the right tool because you are reasoning about aggregate work, not about one person waiting.

Rebuilt the support console's permission model around per-action scopes instead of a single support role that could do everything a customer could do plus impersonation. The old model was built for a five-person support team who all did the same job; we now have three tiers who do quite different things, and the front line did not need the ability to issue refunds or change account ownership. Scopes are declared alongside each console action as a decorator argument and the set of valid scopes is enumerated in `support/scopes.py`, so adding an action without a scope fails at import rather than defaulting to permissive. Impersonation is now its own scope, requires a reason string that is stored with the session, and notifies the affected customer's account owner by email. That last part was contested — support felt it would generate confused replies — and we shipped it anyway with softer wording. Confused replies have been rare and the transparency is worth them. The migration briefly broke two workflows where front-line agents had been informally doing tier-two work, which was itself a useful finding about how the team was actually operating versus how we thought it was.

`/readyz` checks the broker connection and issues a Redis PING; `/livez` returns 200 as long as the event loop is turning and touches no dependency at all. The split is load-bearing and someone well-meaning tries to undo it about once a year. During the `redis-cache` failover in April, both probes pointed at the dependency-checking handler, so every pod in every service failed liveness at the same instant and Kubernetes restarted the entire fleet — turning a forty-second cache blip into an eleven-minute outage, most of it cold start and reconnect storm. Liveness should only answer whether the process is wedged, because the only remedy it has is a restart and a restart will never fix a dependency being down. Readiness is allowed to be fussy, because removing a pod from rotation is cheap and reversible. Consumers additionally report not-ready while draining, which is what makes the rolling deploy behave.

The local Postgres for development comes from `docker-compose.dev.yml` in each repo and is published on host port `55432`, not 5432. Two reasons: several laptops already had a Homebrew postgres listening on the default port left over from a previous job's setup, and the failure mode when your app silently connects to the wrong server is genuinely awful — schema mismatches that present as application bugs. A non-default port makes an accidental connection fail loudly and immediately instead. `.envrc` exports the connection string built from that port, and each repo uses its own database name inside the same container (`larkspur_api_dev`, `edge_agent_dev`) so running two stacks at once does not mean running two servers. The container has no volume mounted, by design: local data is disposable, `make db-reset` drops and re-seeds from the fixtures under `scripts/seed/`, and anyone who wants durable local data can add a volume in a personal compose override. Treating the local database as throwaway removed a whole category of "my local data got weird" debugging.

Required every service to commit a resolved lockfile, and made CI fail if the lockfile is out of date relative to the manifest. Two of our older services had been installing from loose version ranges, which meant that a rebuild in March and a rebuild in April produced different binaries with no record of why. That bit us when a transitive HTTP library shipped a behavioural change in a patch release and one service started sending a header it hadn't before. The check is a single step that runs the installer in a frozen mode and diffs; the invocation is `make deps-check` and it is wired into the default CI target so nobody has to remember it. The harder part was social: the loose ranges existed because updating them was painful, and we had to pair that with a scheduled bump job so the lockfiles don't calcify into a different problem. Reproducibility was worth it. When we now investigate a behaviour change between two deploys, the dependency graph is a fixed input rather than an unknown, and that has cut investigation time on a couple of confusing incidents from hours to minutes.

`make doctor` was written after a support thread that ran three days and ended with a `.venv` pointing at an interpreter mise had garbage-collected. It checks the things that fail confusingly rather than loudly: that installed runtime versions match `.mise.toml`, that direnv is hooked and the `.envrc` is allowed, that the dev database container is listening on its mapped port, that `.venv/bin/python` resolves to a real binary of the pinned version, and that there is more than 10GB free. Each failed check prints its remediation command on the following line, and the target exits non-zero, so it can be the first thing anyone asks for in a support thread instead of the fourth. The rule we settled on is that any environment problem costing two people more than an hour earns a doctor check, written in the same session as the fix while the failure mode is still understood. It is now the first line of the onboarding troubleshooting section, and the flow chart that used to live there is gone.

Every repo exposes the same five Make targets and nothing about a repo's internals leaks into how you invoke it: `make bootstrap` takes a fresh clone to a runnable state, `make dev` starts the local stack, `make test`, `make check` for lint plus types, and `make fmt`. `make help` prints the target list by parsing the `##` comment after each target name, which is why every target carries one. The convention came out of noticing that three repos had three different ways to start a dev server — a shell script, an npm script, and a documented compose incantation — and that the cost was never learning them, it was knowing which one applied where. Underneath, the targets are thin; the Go repo's `make test` is a single line calling the toolchain directly. The Makefile is a naming convention, not an abstraction layer, and we push back on adding logic there that would read better as a script under `scripts/`.

Every CI job now shells out to a make target instead of carrying inline steps. `make lint`, `make test`, `make build` and `make image` exist in the same form in each service root, and the workflow files are nearly empty as a result. The rule we agreed on: no more than one line of shell inside a workflow step, and anything longer belongs in the `Makefile` where a developer can run it. This came out of a week where three separate people could not reproduce a CI failure locally, because the failing command in the YAML had accumulated flags and environment tweaks that existed nowhere else in the repo. Portability was the secondary win. When we moved the runner pool, almost nothing in the job definitions had to change, because the interesting logic was already on the other side of a make target. The cost is that make is now load bearing and has its own failure mode; `make -n` runs in the pre-merge job to catch recipes referencing targets that no longer exist.

Enabled the merge queue on dispatch-api's default branch and trimmed the required checks down to four: lint, unit tests, build, and the contract test. Before the queue, every pull request was green against a base that had already moved by the time it merged, and the branch broke perhaps twice a month from combinations no individual change could have caught — two edits that were each correct against yesterday's schema. The queue re-runs the required set against the prospective merge result, which is the only check that answers the question we actually care about. Trimming the required list was the other half of the work: we had accumulated nine required contexts, several of them advisory leftovers, and a queue running nine suites per candidate merges nothing before lunch. The required list is declared in `.github/settings.yml` so changing it is a reviewed pull request, which stops gates being added quietly by whoever was annoyed most recently.

Locked down Prometheus metric naming: every metric we emit is `karsten_<subsystem>_<thing>_<unit>`, counters end in `_total`, durations are `_seconds` as a float and never milliseconds, sizes are `_bytes`. So `karsten_ingest_messages_received_total` and `karsten_dispatch_request_duration_seconds`, and never `karsten_dispatch_latency_ms`.

The unit rule earned itself twice over. We had a panel adding two counters that turned out to be milliseconds and seconds, which read as plausible nonsense for a month. Standardising on base units means rate() and histogram_quantile() output is directly comparable across services without anyone remembering a conversion.

Enforcement is a regex check in `scripts/check_metric_names.py`, run in CI alongside `promtool check rules`, matching against the exported registry in unit tests. It only catches new metrics — the legacy set that predates the rule is grandfathered in an allowlist at the bottom of that file, which is deliberately ugly so people are motivated to shrink it. Roughly twenty entries remain, mostly on the older Python services where renaming means breaking dashboards nobody has volunteered to update.

Consolidated on mise for runtime version management across every Larkspur repo in March 2026, retiring the mix of pyenv, nvm and asdf that had accumulated one tool per language. Each repo now commits a `.mise.toml` at its root pinning exact patch versions — larkspur-api carries `python = "3.12.7"`, larkspur-web carries `node = "22.11.0"`, edge-agent carries `go = "1.23.4"` — and the only post-clone step is `mise install`. The reason for exact patches rather than ranges was a two-day debugging session where a 3.12.3 laptop and a 3.12.7 laptop disagreed about a datetime parsing edge case and nobody thought to compare interpreter builds. Version drift now surfaces as a mise warning when you cd into the directory instead of as a mystery three hours later. Activation lives in the shell rc via `eval "$(mise activate zsh)"`, which is the one line we ask people to add by hand; everything else the bootstrap target installs. We deliberately did not adopt mise's task runner even though it would work — Make stays the task entrypoint — because the whole point was having one obvious place to look for commands rather than two overlapping ones.

Replaced the flat "error rate above one percent for five minutes" alert with multi-window burn-rate alerting against the 99.5 percent availability target for the dispatch path. Two recording rules feed it, `slo:dispatch_errors:ratio_rate1h` and `slo:dispatch_errors:ratio_rate6h`, both defined in `observability/rules/slo_dispatch.yaml`. The page fires when the one-hour window exceeds a 14.4x burn rate and the six-hour window also exceeds 6x; the second condition is what kills the flapping, since a ninety-second blip can blow through the fast window but cannot move the slow one. A separate ticket-severity rule watches 3x over six hours with a one-day confirmation window, which catches the slow bleed that a five-minute threshold never noticed.

The honest reason for adopting burn rates was not elegance, it was arguments. The old threshold had been renegotiated four times because one percent means something different at 20 requests per second than at 2000, and every renegotiation was a debate with no principled answer. Anchoring on the error budget turned the question into arithmetic: how fast are we spending the quarter's allowance.

The browser end-to-end suite is not a merge gate. It runs after merge on the default branch and again before the release cut, and its failures are triaged rather than blocking anyone. This was contested and the decision came down to arithmetic. The suite takes around twenty-two minutes, and over a quarter we measured its unique catch rate — failures that no cheaper test also caught — as low enough that gating merges on it cost far more aggregate waiting than the defects it prevented would have cost to fix forward. What we committed to in exchange is that a red end-to-end run is treated as urgent rather than as background noise, and that the release owner will not cut a tag over a red run without writing down why. Without that second half the decision would just be an elaborate way of ignoring a test suite we paid to build.

Stopped giving design partners access to nightly builds. The intent was good — earlier feedback, closer collaboration — but in practice two of the three partners pinned a nightly and then ran it for months, and reported bugs against a build corresponding to no release at all, sometimes against a state of the code that had since been rewritten twice. Reproducing those reports cost more engineering time than the feedback returned, and the reports were systematically about half-finished work rather than about anything we had decided to ship. Partners now receive a weekly pre-release cut from the release branch, with notes, and an explicit statement that it is a candidate rather than something to build against for the long term. Feedback volume dropped noticeably and its usefulness went up, which was exactly the trade we were hoping to make.

Eliminated the last three shared administrative accounts, the ones whose passwords lived in the vault and were used by whoever needed them. The argument for keeping them was continuity — the accounts predated most of the current team and owned things nobody wanted to touch. The argument against won: when the audit log says the shared account did something, you have learned nothing about who did it, and that is precisely the log line you most want to be informative. Each shared account was replaced by a named role that individuals assume, with the assumption itself logged. The migration was tedious rather than difficult; the hard part was tracking down every automation that was authenticating as one of them, which took three weeks of grepping and one deliberate breakage to flush out a job nobody had documented. We accepted one lasting exception, a vendor console that genuinely does not support multiple users on our contract tier, and that one has its credential checked out through a process that records who took it and requires a return. It's clumsy. It is also the honest answer, rather than pretending the problem doesn't exist.

The Neovim Python setup runs two language servers, and the split of responsibility is written down explicitly in `~/.config/nvim/lua/plugins/lsp.lua`: basedpyright owns types, hover and go-to-definition with `typeCheckingMode = "basic"`, and ruff owns lint diagnostics, quick fixes and formatting. basedpyright's own formatting and organize-imports capabilities are switched off in its on_attach, and ruff's hover is switched off, because with both enabled a format-on-save reordered imports twice and occasionally produced a diff against itself. Basic mode rather than strict was a deliberate concession: strict lit up the older ingestion modules with several hundred errors nobody was going to fix, and a permanent wall of red diagnostics is functionally the same as no diagnostics. Format on save runs through a filter that only lets ruff's formatter act, and the ruff version is pinned in the repo's dev dependency group, so the editor and the commit hook cannot disagree about what formatted means. This config is offered, not enforced — it sits in the shared dotfiles for anyone who wants a working Python setup in ten minutes rather than an evening.

Made the weekly rotation handoff a live fifteen-minute conversation rather than a written summary posted to a channel. The written version was faithfully produced every week and almost never read, and we could tell because the same context kept getting rediscovered by each successive person on the rotation. The live version forces the outgoing person to actually explain what they're worried about, and more importantly it lets the incoming person ask the question that the written summary never anticipated. Typical duration is under ten minutes; the weeks where it runs long are the weeks something is genuinely unresolved, which is useful signal in itself. We still keep a written record, but it is now notes taken during the conversation rather than a document composed in advance, and its purpose is archival rather than communicative. The one thing we insisted on is that it happens even when nothing happened during the week, because a handoff you skip when things are calm is a handoff you're out of practice at when things aren't. Attendance has been essentially universal, which surprised the person who proposed it and expected to have to chase people.

Every tracker issue carries exactly one `area/*` label and exactly one `kind/*` label — `area/ingest`, `area/insights`, `area/console`, `area/platform` on one axis, `kind/bug`, `kind/feature`, `kind/chore`, `kind/interrupt` on the other. The free-form labels that had accumulated over three years were deleted in a single pass; there were sixty-one of them, forty of which appeared on fewer than four issues. Two orthogonal axes is the smallest taxonomy that answers the two questions cycle planning actually asks: who owns this, and what kind of load is it. Anything more expressive belongs in the issue body, where it can be a sentence instead of a guess at someone else's vocabulary. Adding a new label value requires a note in the planning channel and takes about a day of nobody objecting; adding a third axis has been proposed twice and declined both times.

Turned down the proposal to stand up a log-structured streaming broker for the tracking firehose. The technical argument was reasonable — replay, retention, multiple independent consumers — and about half of it we currently fake with a fan-out exchange and per-consumer queues. The reason for no was ownership: nobody was volunteering to learn a second broker's operational failure modes, and we already carry one whose failure modes we understand, imperfectly, under pressure. Adding a second messaging technology doubles the surface area the team has to be competent across while the team stays the same size. We wrote down the conditions for revisiting: a named owner, a second real use case the current setup genuinely cannot serve, and a migration path for the first one that does not need a flag day. If the analytics group ends up running one for their own reasons, that changes the calculation, because then the operational knowledge already exists somewhere in the building and we would be borrowing rather than building it.

Migrated all span attributes onto OpenTelemetry semantic conventions after two years of bespoke names. The concrete pain was that `dispatch-api` tagged spans with `endpoint`, the Go services used `path`, and the Python planner used `route` — so any cross-service query needed a three-way OR and nobody remembered the third one. Everything now uses `http.route` with the templated path (never the raw URL, which is unbounded), `service.name` set from the deployment rather than hardcoded, and `messaging.destination.name` for the event bus.

The cutover ran as a dual-emit for six weeks: instrumentation wrote both the old and new attribute, dashboards and saved queries were moved over one at a time, and the old attributes were removed only after a search showed zero references. That is slower than a flag day but it meant no incident-time query broke, which was the whole risk.

The one place we deliberately diverge is our own `karsten.tenant_id`, which has no convention equivalent. The rule adopted alongside this: custom attributes must live under the company prefix, so it is always obvious at a glance whether an attribute is portable or ours.

The house rule for paging alerts is that they describe a symptom a customer could notice, not a cause an engineer might care about. Cause alerts — a pod restarting, a cache hit rate falling, a replica lagging — became notifications routed to a team channel, and only the symptom alerts wake anyone.

The reasoning came out of a bad month. We had eleven cause alerts covering the dispatch path, and the night a regional carrier had a routing problem, nine of them fired within four minutes while the actual customer impact was a partial failure on one endpoint. Whoever was looking spent the first twenty minutes triaging alerts instead of the outage. Meanwhile the failure modes we had never imagined produced no page at all, because you can only enumerate causes you have already met, whereas there are only a handful of ways a service fails from the outside: too slow, too many errors, or not answering.

Cause signals are not worthless — they are how you find the answer once you are already looking. They are just terrible at deciding whether to look.

We hold releases for the two weeks around the pre-holiday freight peak, when our customers' volumes roughly triple and their tolerance for anything surprising drops to zero. The freeze is not absolute — fixes for active customer-impacting problems ship, with the on-duty engineering lead's agreement — but everything else waits, including changes people are confident about. That confidence is the trap: every change that caused trouble in previous peaks was one somebody was confident about. Teams plan around the freeze now and it has quietly become the natural window for the cleanup work that never fits otherwise, which is the unintended benefit that stops people resenting it. Freeze dates go out in September so nobody schedules a launch into them and then argues for an exception.

Each two-week cycle gets its own file in the handbook repo — `planning/2026-c07.md` — holding the committed list and a stretch list, one line per item with a tracker link and a named owner. The committed list freezes at kickoff. Adding something afterwards requires taking something out, and the swap is appended to a log at the bottom of the file with a one-line reason. The tracker always showed what was in flight but never what had been promised, so at cycle end there was no honest way to say whether we had done what we said. Six cycles of swap logs turned out to be the most useful planning artefact we have: the pattern in them, mostly inbound work from the console team, is what justified the shield rotation. The file is never retroactively tidied to make a cycle look better.

Scheduled sweeps take a Postgres advisory lock rather than relying on one replica being special: the manifest sweep wraps its run in `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('manifest_sweep'))` and exits quietly when it cannot acquire it. All three API replicas carry the in-process scheduler, so three copies of the sweep were running every hour, each seeing the others' half-finished work. Mostly harmless, right up until the run that produced three copies of an EDI acknowledgement and the carrier rejected the whole batch. Advisory locks were chosen over a Redis lock here specifically because the work is transactional against the same database: the lock releases with the transaction, including when the pod is killed mid-run, and there is no lease duration to guess at and no fencing to get wrong. Where the work is not database-bound we use a Redis lock with a fencing token instead. The rule underneath both: a periodic job must assume it is running on every replica simultaneously and make that safe itself.

The protobuf toolchain is pinned and the generated code is committed. `tools/protoc-version.txt` holds the exact version, the generation script refuses to run against anything else, and `make proto` regenerates into `gen/`, which is checked in. The trigger was a pull request whose diff carried four hundred lines of generated churn because the author had a different protoc installed — the review was effectively impossible and the real change was six lines buried in it. Committing the output is the part people still argue about. The argument that won: consumers of the repo, including CI jobs that only build one service, should not need a code generator installed to compile, and a generated file in the tree is diffable evidence of what the wire format actually is at a given commit. `make proto-check` runs in CI and fails if regeneration produces a diff, so the committed output cannot drift from the schema.

Added an explicit override forcing a single version of the crypto library across the whole dependency graph, because three different direct dependencies were pulling three different minor versions and the resolver's choice varied between the API service and the batch worker. That produced a genuinely confusing bug where a token minted by one service failed validation in the other, roughly one time in forty, tracking a padding behaviour that changed between the two versions. The override lives in the root manifest under the resolutions block and is annotated with a comment pointing at the incident ticket, because an unexplained override is the kind of thing a future maintainer removes while tidying. We also added a test that asserts a token minted by the shared helper validates under the same helper, which sounds trivial and would have caught this in about ten seconds had it existed. The general lesson we took: for any library where two of our services must agree on a wire format, the version is a cross-service contract and should be pinned centrally rather than resolved independently per service. We audited for other cases of this and found one more, the protobuf runtime, which got the same treatment preemptively.

Added the postgres exporter with a custom query file at `deploy/exporters/pg_queries.yaml` so database health is visible in the same Grafana as everything else, instead of requiring someone to open a psql session during an incident. The queries that earned their place are three: per-statement mean and total time from `pg_stat_statements`, dead tuple counts and time since last autovacuum per table, and the age of the oldest running transaction.

The autovacuum panel is the one that has paid for the whole exercise. Table bloat on the trip events table had been creeping up for weeks, autovacuum was being cancelled repeatedly by a long-running analytics query, and the first symptom anyone noticed was a gradual latency drift on the tracking endpoints that nobody had connected to the database. Dead tuples had been climbing on a graph that did not exist yet.

We alert on oldest transaction age above thirty minutes, which is far above anything legitimate here and catches the forgotten open transaction before it blocks vacuum. Statement-level stats stay on the dashboard without an alert — they are for investigation, and any threshold we tried produced noise during normal batch windows.

Changed the postmortem template so the timeline is written and agreed before anyone writes a word of analysis. We kept producing documents where the narrative had already decided what went wrong by paragraph two, and the timeline was then assembled to support that narrative — which meant we consistently missed the ten minutes between the first alert and the first human response, because that gap didn't fit the story anyone wanted to tell. Now the first working session is purely reconstruction: what happened, at what time, according to what evidence, with no causal language allowed. Only once everyone signs off on the timeline does the second session start on contributing factors. It takes longer and people grumbled about it for the first two incidents. Then a postmortem produced an action item nobody expected — our alert routing had been silently dropping notifications for one team for six weeks — and it only surfaced because the timeline made the gap visible before anyone had a theory to defend. That converted the skeptics. The rule now is that a postmortem with an incomplete timeline doesn't get scheduled for review.

Each repo ships `.github/pull_request_template.md` with two required headings: "Why now" and "How this was verified". Why now is the one that earns its keep — it catches the change that is technically fine but was triggered by a misreading of a ticket, and it gives the reviewer the frame to evaluate against instead of reverse-engineering intent from the diff. How this was verified is prose, not a checkbox: which command was run, against what data, and what was observed. "CI is green" is not an answer to it. A reviewer is entitled to hand a PR back on an empty verification section without reading the code at all, and that is not considered rude here. The template stays two headings long on purpose; an earlier six-section version got filled in with dashes within a month, which is worse than having no template because it looks like compliance.

`.pre-commit-config.yaml` is committed in every repo and the hook set is chosen against a wall-clock budget: the whole run stays under three seconds on a typical diff. That buys ruff and ruff-format, prettier scoped to the web source directory, shellcheck, a trailing-whitespace fixer, and `check-added-large-files` with `--maxkb=512` after someone committed a 40MB packet capture. Nothing that needs a full type check or a test run is allowed in there. `pre-commit install` runs inside `make bootstrap` so nobody has to remember it, and the tool versions in the config are pinned to the same versions in the dev dependency group, so the hook and the editor can never disagree about what needs fixing. The three-second number is not a preference, it is a threshold we measured our way to: the previous hook set took about nineteen seconds and the observable result was that half the team had learned the flag that skips hooks entirely.

Settled an argument that kept recurring: when we suspect a credential may have leaked but aren't sure, we revoke first and rotate second, rather than rotating quietly and hoping. The rotate-only path feels lower-drama because nothing breaks, but it leaves the old credential valid until it expires naturally, which for some of our integrations is ninety days. Revoking causes an immediate, visible failure that we can respond to in minutes with a fresh credential, and the failure itself is diagnostic — it tells us exactly which systems were using that credential, which we are frequently wrong about. The cost is a short outage of whatever depended on it. We decided that cost is acceptable because the alternative is an unknown window where an attacker holds a working key and we've convinced ourselves we handled it. The team lead pushed back initially on the grounds that this makes people reluctant to report suspicions. Fair concern, and the answer was to make reporting blameless and to treat the resulting blip as the cost of a healthy process rather than as an incident with a postmortem. Six months in, nobody has complained about the noise and we've caught two genuinely leaked keys this way.

Shared packages publish under the `@halyard/` scope to the internal registry, mapped in the repo-level `.npmrc`. Publishing is a CI-only operation: the release workflow holds the credential and runs `npm publish --provenance`, and the registry refuses developer tokens for that scope outright. The rule exists because a package once went out from a laptop with uncommitted local changes in it, and the version consumers resolved could not be reproduced from any commit in the repository — we found out weeks later while chasing a bug that existed in exactly one published tarball. Provenance attestations let a consumer check which workflow run and which commit produced a given version, and that has turned out to be worth more internally than externally: it is how we answer where a particular build of the shared component library came from without interrupting anyone. Version bumps are made by the release script from the tag, so the published version and the git tag cannot disagree.

External availability is probed from two regions and the page requires both to be failing. The blackbox job is `probe_public_edge` in the prometheus config, using the `http_2xx_dispatch` module which posts a synthetic assignment and asserts on the response body rather than just the status code — an early version only checked for 200 and cheerfully reported green through an incident where the edge was returning a cached error page with a 200.

Single-region probing gave us four false pages in six weeks, every one of them a network problem between the prober and the edge rather than an actual outage. Requiring agreement between two geographically separate probers eliminated all four without, as far as we can tell, hiding anything real: a genuine edge failure shows up in both within one scrape interval. If exactly one prober is failing, that is a warning to a channel, since it usually does mean something is wrong, just not with us.

The probe runs on a 15s interval and is exempt from the 30s global default, because for an availability signal the detection delay matters more than the storage cost.

Stopped treating production read access as a seniority marker and started treating it as a specific tool for specific jobs. We had accumulated a situation where everyone above a certain level had it, largely because it was easier to grant than to explain why not, and the practical result was around thirty people with the ability to read customer records and roughly four who ever needed to. The change was to grant it per-need with an expiry, defaulting to a working week, renewable by asking. Nobody lost the ability to do their job. What they lost was the standing ability, which is different, and the objection that this would slow down debugging turned out to be mostly hypothetical — in the six months since, the median time from request to grant has been under twenty minutes during working hours. The cultural piece mattered more than the mechanism. We had to say explicitly and repeatedly that having access removed was not a signal of distrust, because the first two rounds of removals generated some genuinely hurt feelings. Framing it as reducing what an attacker gets from any single compromised account, rather than as anything about the individual, was what eventually landed.

Moved the global Prometheus scrape interval from 15s to 30s in `deploy/prometheus/prometheus.yml` during the March cardinality squeeze. The trigger was head-block memory on the prod Prometheus pair sitting above 40 GiB and compaction falling behind during peak dispatch hours. Nothing we page on evaluates faster than a two-minute `for:` clause, so the extra resolution was collected and thrown away every cycle. Two job groups kept the old cadence: the blackbox probe job, because probe latency is a leading indicator we graph at second resolution, and `ingest-gateway`, whose request rate goes from idle to twenty thousand per second when a regional fleet reconnects after a tower outage. Everything else — sidecars, node exporter, kube-state — went to 30s. Sample ingest dropped about 45 percent, memory settled near 24 GiB, and no dashboard visibly changed except a handful of one-minute rate() panels that turned jagged; those were rewritten onto a five-minute window. The real cost is that spikes shorter than thirty seconds are now invisible in metrics, which is why the team guidance is to reach for traces, not graphs, when chasing anything sub-minute.

The artifact that reaches production is bit for bit the one that was exercised in pre-production; promotion moves a pointer and never triggers a rebuild. This sounds obvious and was not how we worked until a release where the production build resolved a different transitive dependency than the tested build had, because the two builds ran days apart and something upstream had moved underneath us. Nothing actually broke, but we could not explain a behaviour difference for most of a day, and that was enough to settle the argument. Building once also means the test results are evidence about the thing that ships rather than about a sibling of it, which is the whole reason we run the tests. The cost is that the promotion machinery has to carry artifacts between environments rather than each environment being self-sufficient, and we took on that complexity knowingly.

Cut the almanac test matrix from four Python versions to two: `3.11`, the oldest we support in production, and `3.13`, the newest we intend to move to. Before deciding we went back through eighteen months of CI history looking for a failure that appeared on an interior version and not on either endpoint, and found none. The interior jobs were pure cost and made up roughly forty percent of the pipeline's wall clock. The endpoints are where the interesting breakage lives anyway: removed deprecations at the bottom, new syntax and changed stdlib behaviour at the top. If a customer ever needs an interior version certified we will add it back for that release rather than carrying it on every run for the rest of time.

Made the quarterly access review consequential by defaulting to removal rather than to retention. The previous version asked managers to confirm their reports' access, and unanswered reviews defaulted to keeping everything, which meant the review was functionally optional and roughly half of it went unanswered. Now an unreviewed grant is revoked at the deadline. The first cycle under the new rule revoked a lot and generated some genuine annoyance, most of which was resolved within a day by people re-requesting what they actually needed — and about a third of the revocations were never re-requested at all, which is the number that justified the change. Response rate on the second cycle was ninety-four percent. The mechanics are handled by the identity platform's campaign feature rather than by anything we built, deliberately, because the last thing we needed was to own a compliance workflow. We do own the report that goes to the auditors, which is generated from the campaign results. The one carve-out is the paging rotation's escalation permissions, which are excluded from auto-revocation for obvious reasons and are instead reviewed manually by the platform lead.

Every quarter we pull the firing history for all paging rules and any rule that fired more than a dozen times without a matching incident record has to be defended by its owner or it is deleted or demoted. This is not a suggestion, it is a scheduled meeting with a list, and the default outcome is deletion.

The forcing function is that alert fatigue is invisible in any dashboard. Nobody files a ticket saying "I have started ignoring the notification channel", they just do it, and you find out during the one incident where the signal was real. Making the review periodic and mechanical means we notice the drift before it costs us.

What we learned running it four times: most noisy rules are not badly thresholded, they are badly scoped. They fire on a real condition that simply is not urgent — a retryable dependency hiccup, a nightly job briefly saturating a worker pool. Demoting those to a channel notification usually satisfies the owner, who mostly wanted to know it happened, not to be woken up. Outright deletion is rarer than expected, maybe one rule in five.

Standing preference: new asynchronous work starts life as a queue consumer, not a cron entry. Cron gives you no retry, no visibility into failure beyond whatever the job managed to log, no backpressure when the previous run is still going, and its concurrency story is optimism. A consumer gets all of that from the broker for free, plus the dead-letter path we already know how to operate and already have tooling for. The genuine exceptions are jobs that really are about time of day — the end-of-day manifest close has to happen at the carrier's cutoff, not whenever a message happens to arrive — and even those take a lock and publish messages rather than doing the work inline. We converted the four legacy jobs on the old scheduler host to this shape over a quarter, and the number of "did that run last night?" questions dropped to roughly zero, which was the actual point. When someone proposes cron for something event-shaped, the counter-question is what happens when it fails at three in the morning.

Local services should be quiet by default. The dev stack prints its startup line, its bound address, and then nothing until something actually happens; debug logging is opt-in per run rather than the default, and the framework loggers that narrate every internal step are turned down specifically in the development configuration. The reason is behavioural rather than technical: when a terminal produces a continuous wall of output, people stop reading it, and then the one line that mattered scrolls past unnoticed. We learned that during a week where a deprecation warning about a misconfigured local setting printed on every single request and nobody saw it, because seeing it would have meant reading the noise. Quiet output also makes the reload loop legible — you can tell at a glance whether the server restarted cleanly, which is most of what anyone wants from that terminal anyway.

Rate quotes for a lane are cached for five minutes, and the flat TTL bit us: a deploy warms every hot lane within a few seconds of each other, so five minutes later they all expire in the same second and `rating-engine` takes a synchronised wall of misses. The TTL is now written as `ttl = 300 + random.randint(0, 90)` at set time, which smears expiry across a ninety-second window. Separately added a single-flight guard, so concurrent misses on the same key wait on one in-flight computation rather than each doing the work. Measured both on the 03:00 warm cycle: origin QPS on the spike dropped from about twenty-four times baseline to roughly three times. Keep the two ideas distinct when reasoning about this later — jitter fixes correlated expiry across keys, single-flight fixes pile-up on one key. They solve different halves of the stampede and we needed both to make the graph flat.

Set `heartbeat = 30` on every RabbitMQ connection after `edi-gateway` consumers went silent for most of a working day without anyone noticing. The old config had heartbeats disabled. The NAT gateway drops idle flows after 350 seconds, so the broker reaped the connection and reassigned its unacked messages while the client still believed it was connected and sat waiting on a socket nothing would ever arrive on. With a thirty-second heartbeat the client notices inside about a minute and reconnects on its own. Also set `blocked_connection_timeout = 300` so a publisher blocked by a broker memory alarm raises instead of hanging forever. The lesson, which we have now learned twice in two different places, is that a TCP connection nobody writes to is indistinguishable from a healthy one until you try to use it, and every network hop between a service and the broker has an idle timer shorter than you assume.

The first code block in every service README must be a command that takes a clean checkout to a running local instance, and by convention that command is `make bootstrap`. A weekly scheduled CI job clones each repo into a bare container image and runs `make bootstrap && make check`, so setup instructions rot loudly rather than silently. The trigger was an ingest-gateway README that had been wrong for five months — three separate people rediscovered the same missing step and fixed it in their own shell history instead of the file. Prose setup instructions decay because nobody follows them twice; a command decays visibly because something executes it. The corollary that people forget: if the bootstrap needs a credential, the README says which credential and where to ask for it, and never how to fabricate a substitute. Anything the job cannot verify — editor settings, optional tooling — goes below the fold under a heading that admits it is unverified.

Service dashboards follow RED — rate, errors, duration — and infrastructure dashboards follow USE — utilisation, saturation, errors. Same three rows, same order, same position, on every board.

This is a consistency decision rather than a claim that these are the only metrics worth watching. Before it, each team's dashboard reflected whatever they had debugged most recently, so opening an unfamiliar service during an incident meant spending the first two minutes learning the layout instead of reading it. Now anyone can open any service board and know that the top-left panel is throughput and the panel beside it is error ratio, without thinking.

Teams may add whatever domain-specific rows they like below the standard three, and most do — the route planner has a solver quality row that means nothing to anyone else and is genuinely useful to its owners. The constraint is only on the top of the board, which is the part strangers read under pressure.

The one place this fits badly is queue-driven workers, where request rate is not the natural unit. Those use arrival rate and drain time in the same slots, which is close enough that the muscle memory still works.

Consolidated Redis access behind one module-level client per process, in `services/common/cache/redis_client.py`. Before this, each request handler in `shipment-api` constructed its own `Redis()` and let garbage collection close it, so the connection count on `redis-cache` tracked request rate rather than pod count — we peaked near 11k connections during the February quote storm, and `CLIENT LIST` was useless for triage because it was all noise. The shared client is created at import time with `max_connections = 64`, which caps the worst case at pods times 64 and leaves headroom under the cluster's configured limit. The pool is not fork-safe, so `manifest-builder`, which pre-forks, calls the reset hook in its post-fork callback; forgetting that gives you two processes sharing one socket and errors that read like data corruption. The why we keep repeating in review: Redis connections are cheap to open and expensive to hold. Idle ones cost buffer memory on the server, they hide the real client count, and they turn a rolling deploy into a reconnect stampede. Constructing an ad-hoc client anywhere outside that module is a review stopper — if you need different timeouts, add a named client to the module instead of a local one at the call site.

The two Redis clusters run deliberately different eviction policies. `redis-cache` uses `maxmemory-policy = allkeys-lru` — everything in it is reconstructible from origin, so dropping the coldest key under memory pressure is exactly right. `redis-state` uses `maxmemory-policy = noeviction`, because it holds distributed locks, dedupe sets for the notification path, and Celery results. Evicting a lock is not a slow answer, it is a wrong one: two workers run the same job and a customer gets two shipment confirmations. With `noeviction` a full state cluster returns write errors instead, which page us, which is the outcome we want. This is also the reason the two workloads are not sharing one cluster despite the cost of running two — no single policy is correct for both, and the failure mode of picking the wrong one is silent. Capacity alarms on the state cluster sit at seventy percent rather than the usual eighty-five for the same reason.

Release notes are written in two sections for two audiences. The upper half is customer-facing: what changed that someone outside would notice, phrased without internal service names and without ticket numbers. The lower half is for us: schema changes, configuration that needs attention on the next deploy, and anything an engineer would want to find later while bisecting a behaviour change. We tried a single merged section and it served neither audience — customers waded through internal noise, and engineers lost the operationally important lines among marketing-adjacent phrasing. Keeping them separate also means the customer half can be handed to support without editing, which was the practical trigger for the change, since support had been rewriting our notes every week anyway and occasionally getting the meaning wrong.

The release owner rotates weekly through everyone who has shipped anything in the last quarter, and is deliberately not tied to whoever is carrying the pager that week. Two reasons. Releasing is a skill with a lot of small implicit knowledge, and concentrating it in one person means the release stops when that person takes a holiday, which is precisely what happened to us before the rotation existed. And the owner needs the standing to hold the train, which is much easier to exercise when it is an ordinary part of everyone's job than when it is one person's permanent responsibility and therefore their reputation. Holding is explicitly not a failure and we say so during every handover, because the first two rotations both shipped things they were privately unsure about rather than be the person who delayed a release.

We cut the release train on Thursday mornings, and the choice is more considered than it looks. Friday was the obvious candidate and we rejected it: a release that misbehaves on Friday afternoon spends the weekend either unattended or eating somebody's Saturday, and the pressure to declare it fine before leaving is exactly the pressure that produces bad judgement calls. Monday was rejected for the opposite reason — fixes that land late on Friday get no soak at all, and Monday mornings are already congested with whatever accumulated over the weekend. Thursday leaves a full working day plus Friday morning to watch the rollout while the people who wrote the code are still at their desks, and it sits far enough from the weekend that nobody is racing a deadline. If the train slips it slips to the following week rather than sliding onto Friday, which we have now had to say out loud several times before it stuck.

Release binaries are built reproducibly: `-trimpath`, `-ldflags '-s -w -buildid='`, `CGO_ENABLED=0`, and `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` derived from the tagged commit's timestamp for the tarball. `make verify-repro` builds twice into separate directories and diffs the sha256 sums. It runs as part of the release workflow only, not on every pull request, because it doubles build time for a property that only matters at the moment we publish. The requirement came out of a customer security review: they wanted to rebuild the artifact from the tag and compare it against what we shipped, and at the time we would have failed that test. Getting there meant removing two build-time timestamp embeds and one absolute path leaking out of an embedded asset. The version metadata that used to be a build date is now the commit sha, which is strictly more useful to anyone reading it.

Retired the Apdex score from the executive dashboard. It had been there since before most of the current team, and the problem was that nobody could explain what a move from 0.94 to 0.91 meant in terms anyone could act on. The score compresses a satisfied threshold, a tolerating threshold, and a failure count into one number, and the compression is where the information goes. Two very different weeks — one with uniformly mediocre latency, one with a sharp outage on a Tuesday — produced nearly identical scores.

We replaced it with the error budget remaining for the quarter, expressed as a percentage and a rough number of minutes. That has the property Apdex lacked: it is directly connected to a decision. Budget nearly spent means slow down on risky changes. Budget healthy means ship.

The secondary reason was that the tolerating threshold was set to four times the satisfied threshold by convention, not by evidence about our users, so the number encoded an assumption nobody had ever checked. If a metric's shape comes from a default in a library rather than from something you measured, it is decoration.

Retros run every second cycle rather than every cycle, and only if at least one person has put an item on the list beforehand. An empty list means the meeting is cancelled that morning and nobody feels bad about it. Weekly retros had degraded into a routine where people invented mild grievances to fill the time, and the resulting actions were the kind nobody intends to do. The other rule: an action taken out of a retro gets a named owner and a tracker entry during the meeting itself, or it is not an action, it is a sentiment. Sentiments are fine and often the most valuable part of the hour, but writing them into a list titled Actions is how a team learns that the list means nothing.

Rollback means redeploying the previously released artifact. It does not mean reverting commits under time pressure and shipping the result, which is a new and untested build wearing the costume of a known-good one. We wrote the distinction down because it is the kind of thing everyone agrees with calmly and then abandons at speed. Under incident conditions the fastest safe action is to put back something that was demonstrably running fine an hour ago, and the revert can be prepared afterwards on a normal branch with normal review. This is also the reason release artifacts are exempt from the storage expiry rules: the rollback path depends on the old artifact still existing, and a rollback that first requires rebuilding from an old tag is not a rollback, it is a build with an audience watching.

Real user monitoring on the dispatcher web console samples at `session_sample_rate = 0.1`, with a boost that captures 100 percent of sessions that hit a JavaScript error or a failed network request. The config lives with the app under `apps/tracking-web/src/observability/rum.ts`.

Ten percent is enough to compute stable page-load percentiles for a user base of a few thousand dispatchers, and full capture on error sessions means every actual complaint has a session recording behind it, which is the only reason RUM justified its cost. Uniform sampling at a rate we could afford would have missed most reported problems.

We strip query strings and set the tenant ID as an attribute rather than letting it appear in URLs, because dispatcher session URLs contain load references that are customer-identifying. That stripping happens client side before anything is sent, not in the backend pipeline, so nothing sensitive crosses the wire in the first place.

One thing we got wrong initially: the boost was implemented as a second sampling decision, so error sessions were captured from the moment of the error onward, missing the interactions that led to it. It now buffers the session from the start and discards the buffer if no error occurs.

Moved CI off the hosted 16-core runners onto a self-managed scale set of bare metal in the Frankfurt cage in Q1, after queue depth in the 09:00-11:00 CET window sat above thirty jobs most mornings and the hosted bill crossed what two boxes cost outright. The scale set is defined in `infra/ci/runners/scaleset.tf` and keeps `min_idle = 6` warm between 07:00 and 19:00 CET, falling to `min_idle = 1` overnight. The warm floor is the whole point: a cold runner spends about ninety seconds pulling the build image before it does any useful work, and six idle machines cost less per month than the aggregate developer wait we were absorbing. Jobs that need more than 32 GB still route to the hosted pool via the `runs-on: hosted-xl` label, because sizing the metal for the worst job would have left it idle most of the day. Scale set changes go through the normal infra review; nobody edits runner config from the provider console, since the scale set reconciles on its next pass and silently reverts it, which cost someone an afternoon before we understood it.

Changed how static analysis findings get closed after noticing that our suppression file had grown to four hundred lines and nobody could say which entries were still meaningful. The new rule: a finding can be closed as fixed, or closed as a false positive with a one-line reason and a code comment at the site, but it cannot be closed by adding a bare entry to the suppression list. Bare entries are now rejected by a check in `scripts/check_suppressions.sh` that requires each line to carry a `reason=` field and an owner. We regenerated the whole file from scratch rather than trying to retroactively annotate the existing entries — that would have been archaeology on findings from three years and two tool versions ago. Regenerating produced sixty-one live findings, of which nine were real and got fixed, and the rest were genuinely false positives from a rule about SQL string construction that our query builder trips constantly. We disabled that one rule globally with a comment explaining why, which is more honest than suppressing its output six hundred times. Total time spent was about two days and the file is now something a person can read.

Started generating a software bill of materials at build time and attaching it to the release artifact, rather than reconstructing one on demand when a customer's procurement team asks. The reconstruct-on-demand approach took a person about three days each time and produced an answer that was accurate for the current tip of the branch rather than for the version the customer was actually running, which is a subtly useless answer. Generation happens in the build stage and the output lands next to the artifact as `sbom.spdx.json`, keyed to the same version string. The real payoff came during the serialization library advisory in April: we could answer "which shipped versions contain the affected package" in about four minutes by querying the stored SBOMs, instead of guessing from release dates. That turned a scramble into a routine notification with an accurate list. Cost was low — the generator adds roughly forty seconds to a build — and the main work was making sure the generator saw the same resolved graph the build did rather than re-resolving, which would have produced a plausible and wrong document. We validated that by diffing the SBOM against the container's installed package list for a week.

Norm we adopted after a retro: when you are screen sharing or driving in a pair session, switch to the high-contrast profile, bump the font two sizes, and turn off terminal transparency. It sounds trivial and it is not. One engineer has low vision and had been silently reconstructing half of what was on screen from context, and two others had simply stopped asking people to zoom in, because asking a third time in the same meeting feels rude. Everyone keeps whatever theme they like for solo work; this applies only when other people are looking at your screen. The practical version is that everybody set up a second terminal and editor profile once, so switching is a keystroke rather than a settings excursion in the middle of a call. The thing that made it stick was making it the presenter's job to switch rather than the viewer's job to ask.

Moved our answers to customer security questionnaires out of a sales folder and into the engineering repo, on the grounds that they are claims about how the system works and should be reviewed by people who know whether they're true. The previous arrangement had sales copying answers forward from the last questionnaire, which meant an answer written in 2023 about our encryption posture was still being sent in 2025 after we'd changed it twice — in one case understating what we actually do, which is embarrassing in a different direction. The canonical answers now live at `docs/security/questionnaire_responses.md`, one section per common question topic, and changing anything in that file requires review from the platform lead. Sales pulls from it rather than from the previous response. We also added a `last_verified` date per section and a reminder that flags anything older than six months, because the failure mode here is not a wrong answer written deliberately but a right answer that quietly became wrong. Nine of the thirty-one sections were stale on the first pass. The overall effect is that answering a questionnaire is now mostly assembly rather than research, which cut turnaround from about a week to a day.

We decided against broker priority levels and use separate queues with their own worker deployments instead. Priorities looked attractive when the expedited shipping work needed to jump the line, but they interact badly with prefetch — a worker sitting on prefetched low-priority messages will not go and fetch the high-priority one that just arrived — and they turn starvation into something you reason about rather than something you can see. With separate queues, capacity becomes an explicit allocation: expedited work has its own pool, and if it is starved that shows up as its own queue metric and its own scaling decision, not as an emergent property of the broker's internal ordering. It costs some idle capacity, which we consider a fair price for a system where "why has this message not been picked up" has an answer you can point at on a dashboard. This came out of the expedited-lane review in the spring and nobody has argued for going back.

Gave every scrape job an explicit series budget after `ingest-gateway` added a `device_id` label and quietly created 1.9 million series in an afternoon. The budget is `max_series_per_job = 25000` unless a service argues for more in review, enforced two ways: a `metric_relabel_configs` block that drops the known-unbounded labels (`device_id`, `trip_id`, `session_id`, raw `path`) at scrape time, and a weekly report from `scripts/top_series.sh` that prints the ten largest jobs by active series and posts the diff against last week. High-cardinality identifiers are not banned from telemetry, they are banned from metrics — they belong on spans, where storage is sampled and the query pattern is point lookup rather than time-series aggregation.

The relabel drop happens on the Prometheus side rather than in service code on purpose: we cannot rely on twenty-odd services shipping a fix simultaneously, and a scrape-side rule protects the store the moment it merges. Services that need a per-device view got a Grafana panel backed by traces instead. Since the rule landed, active series across prod has stayed inside 1.4 million with room to spare.

Built a reconciler that compares the service accounts that exist in the cloud project against the ones declared in our infrastructure repo, and files an issue for anything in one set and not the other. We had drifted badly: the audit found nineteen accounts nobody could explain, four of which had been created for a proof of concept that shipped in 2023 and were still holding write permissions. The reconciler runs nightly via `scripts/reconcile_service_accounts.py` and posts a diff. Undeclared accounts get a fourteen-day grace period before we disable rather than delete, because deleting is unrecoverable and disabling is a phone call away from being undone. Declared-but-missing accounts are a harder error and page the platform rotation, since that usually means somebody deleted something the deploy depends on. The one design decision worth remembering: the reconciler does not auto-remediate. It was tempting, but an automated actor with permission to delete service accounts is exactly the blast radius we were trying to shrink. It reports, a human acts. That's slower and it's the right call for something with this much destructive potential.

New engineers do not set up their machine alone from the doc. They pair with a buddy for the first afternoon, and the buddy's actual job is to notice the places where the doc is wrong or assumes knowledge, because those spots are invisible to anyone who has been here six months. The checklist exists and should be followed, but the doc is not the mechanism; the pairing is. Every gap the buddy notices gets fixed the same day, which is the only reason the doc is still accurate. The target is that a new engineer opens a small pull request on day two — not because speed is the point, but because it exercises the whole path end to end: clone, environment, tests, local run, branch, review, merge. Every time that has not happened by day three, it has turned out that something in the environment was quietly broken rather than that the person was going slowly.

The shared configuration stops where taste begins, and being explicit about that boundary has headed off a recurring argument. Shared: whitespace, formatter behaviour, language server setup, the tool baseline — anything that affects what lands in the repository or what another person sees in a diff. Personal: keybindings, prompt appearance, aliases, colour schemes, window management, whether you use a multiplexer at all. Nobody reviews anyone's personal configuration and nobody is expected to justify it. The reason for drawing the line out loud is that a shared tooling repository invites contributions of the form "here is my alias file, should this be shared", and every one of those we accepted became a small maintenance obligation plus a small imposition on people who did not want it. The compromise that works is that personal configurations are visible — most people's are readable by teammates — so borrowing is easy, but nothing personal is ever installed by default.

All outbound HTTP in the Python services goes through the shared client in `services/common/http/session.py`. It is built once per process with `max_keepalive_connections = 20` and `keepalive_expiry = 25`, the expiry chosen deliberately below the thirty-second idle close that both Northline and Corvus Post use — reusing a socket the peer has already closed produced a steady trickle of remote-disconnect retries that we blamed on carrier flakiness for two months. Constructing a client per request was also costing a full TLS handshake, roughly seventy to ninety milliseconds against the carrier endpoints, on every single call.
