Timeouts are explicit on the shared client: connect three seconds, read twenty, write ten, pool five, with per-call overrides for label rendering, which legitimately takes longer. The pool timeout matters more than people expect. Without it, one slow carrier turns into unbounded waiting for a connection slot, and the symptom surfaces in an unrelated code path that happens to share the pool. New integrations that need different limits add a named client in that module rather than building one at the call site.

Release images are signed at publish time and the production cluster refuses unsigned ones. Signing is keyless against the CI workload identity, so there is no long-lived signing key for anyone to leak or misplace. The admission policy lives in `policy/verify-image.yaml` and matches the production namespaces only, leaving the internal cluster unrestricted so experiments stay cheap. The motivating incident was not an attack. During a long outage someone built an image on a laptop, pushed it and rolled it out, and afterwards we could not establish what source it had been built from because the working tree was gone. Admission verification makes that path fail loudly at the moment it is attempted, rather than three weeks later during a review when the useful context has evaporated. The policy is fail-closed. We discussed a warn-only period and decided against it, on the grounds that a warning in a rollout log is a warning nobody reads.

The roadmap commits six weeks out and no further. Everything beyond that horizon is on an explicitly labelled maybe list with no dates attached, and we decline to attach dates to it even when asked politely. Quarterly roadmaps had been renegotiated so frequently that the document stopped being a plan and became a record of negotiations, which is a strictly worse artefact — it was long, everyone knew it was fiction, and it still generated arguments about commitments nobody had actually made. Six weeks is roughly three cycles, long enough for another team to plan against and short enough that we are usually right. The tradeoff we accepted, with some discomfort, is that the sales side genuinely wanted longer visibility. What we offered instead was a standing commitment about what we would not change out from under them, which turned out to be most of what they needed the dates for anyway.

Rather than negotiate a latency target for each of the roughly ninety endpoints, we sorted them into three classes and gave each class one target. Interactive endpoints are anything a driver or dispatcher waits on with a spinner. Background endpoints are things triggered by a system and consumed later. Bulk endpoints are report and export paths where a human has already accepted that it will take a while.

The per-endpoint approach had collapsed under its own weight — after two months we had targets for eleven endpoints, all of them set by whoever last complained, and no principle connecting them. Classes made the question answerable in review by anyone: which of these three is it. Where an endpoint genuinely does not fit, that is treated as a signal about the API design more often than about the SLO, and twice it led to splitting an endpoint that was doing two different jobs.

Availability targets stayed per service rather than per class, because availability failures are almost always shared infrastructure rather than one handler, so a per-endpoint number would just be the same number written many times.

Incident write-ups embed dashboard snapshots, not dashboard links. A link is a promise about the future that the dashboard does not keep: panels get edited, queries get renamed, the underlying data ages out of raw resolution, and six months later the link renders a board that looks nothing like what the responder saw. We reviewed an incident where the linked graph had been rewritten twice since, and the discussion drifted into arguing about a picture nobody in the room had actually looked at during the event.

A snapshot freezes the series data at the time it was taken, so it stays a faithful record of what was on screen when the decision was made — which is the point of a write-up. Judging a past decision against a graph that has since been improved is unfair and teaches nothing.

The practical friction is that snapshots have to be taken while the incident is live, and people forget in the middle of it. So the incident template has a step for it and whoever is scribing owns it, which works about three times in four. When it is missed the write-up says so explicitly rather than quietly substituting a link.

Investigation spikes are timeboxed to three days and the deliverable is a written memo ending in a recommendation, never a branch. Whatever code got written during the spike is deleted, deliberately and visibly. The reason is that spike code is optimised for learning fast — no error handling, no tests, whatever shortcut answered the question — and the moment it survives into a branch, the pressure to salvage it rather than rewrite it becomes very hard to resist, especially when the spike ran long. We lost a quarter to exactly that on the insights side once. Writing the memo also forces the person to state what they now believe and how confident they are, which is the actual output; the throwaway code was only ever the instrument. If the recommendation is accepted, implementation is planned as normal work with normal standards, and the memo gets linked from the resulting design document.

The carrier-document path is the last thing still on SQS, inherited along with the S3 event notification it hangs off. Its `visibility_timeout = 210` is deliberate: observed p99 processing for a large manifest is about sixty-eight seconds, and we set the timeout at roughly three times that. At the old sixty-second value, big manifests were redelivered while the first attempt was still running, which produced duplicate PDFs in the output bucket and a support ticket about double-billed print jobs. The alternative — extending visibility with heartbeats from inside the handler — was rejected as more moving parts than a path handling a few thousand messages a day deserves. If processing time creeps upward, the fix is to re-measure p99 and raise the timeout, not to add heartbeating. Writing this down because the number looks arbitrary sitting in Terraform and somebody will eventually want to round it to 180.

Made the identity provider's groups the single source of truth for authorization across every internal system, and forbade any service from maintaining its own user list. Before this, the wiki had its own admin list, the monitoring stack had its own, and the ticket tracker had a third — so an offboarded engineer stayed an admin in two of the three for weeks. The mapping now lives in `infra/identity/group_mappings.yaml`, one entry per group, listing which systems it grants what in. Adding a system to that file is a PR that a second person approves; there is no console-clicking path anymore, and where a service allowed one we disabled it. Onboarding and offboarding are consequently a single change to group membership in the IdP and everything else follows within the sync interval, which is fifteen minutes. The exception we allowed: break-glass local accounts on two systems, documented, with credentials in the shared vault and an alert that fires whenever one is used. That alert has fired exactly once in a year, during a legitimate IdP outage, which is roughly the frequency we designed for.

The daily standup meeting was removed and replaced with a threaded post that people write and read whenever their day starts. It was a genuinely bad meeting for a team spread across three timezones: it happened at a time that suited exactly one of them, and the westmost engineers were reporting on work they had not yet done that day. The information a standup carries is low-urgency by nature — nothing said in one has ever needed to be heard within the hour — so making it asynchronous costs almost nothing. What we deliberately kept is the one thing standups were bad at anyway: the weekly synchronous slot where two people who suspect they are working on overlapping problems can talk it through properly, which never fit into a round-robin of thirty-second updates.

Standardised the default prompt on starship, shipped as `~/.config/starship.toml` through the dotfiles source. The config is deliberately short: directory, git branch, the language version when the directory has a manifest, and a red exit-code segment. We set `command_timeout = 1000` because the default 500ms kept firing timeout warnings in the web repo, where the working tree is large enough that a full git status scan is slow, and then disabled the git status counts entirely and kept only the branch name — the counts were the slow part and nobody was reading them anyway. The prompt is a baseline, not a mandate: it is what you get if you do nothing, and anyone who prefers their own is welcome to keep it, since no tooling anywhere parses the prompt. The reason for having a default at all is pairing and screen shares. When everyone's prompt puts the branch in the same place, you stop having to ask which branch the other person is on.

Statement timeouts are attached to database roles rather than connection strings, so they survive a service forgetting to configure itself: `ALTER ROLE app_rw SET statement_timeout = '8s'`, `app_ro` at `30s`, and the reporting role at `15min`. Eight seconds is generous for anything on the request path — if a shipment lookup takes longer than that, the query is wrong and the user gave up two refreshes ago. Before this, one unindexed filter added to the search endpoint held a connection open for minutes at a time, and the visible symptom was unrelated endpoints timing out, which sent three of us chasing the wrong service for an hour. Setting the guard on the role means a psql session, a one-off backfill script, and a brand new service all inherit it without anyone remembering to opt in. The reporting role's long timeout is intentional and exists only on the replica, where a slow analytical query cannot hurt anything a customer is waiting on.

Story points were abandoned after two quarters of trying. We now count items and track how many of them finish in a cycle, and that is the entire estimation practice. The failure was not that the numbers were inaccurate — everyone expects that — it was that they stopped being estimates. Points were negotiated rather than assessed, because a larger number bought slack and a smaller one bought approval, and once the velocity figure appeared on a slide outside engineering it became a target and immediately stopped measuring anything. Counting items is theoretically worse: items are wildly different sizes and the count says nothing about difficulty. In practice it is honest, costs nothing to produce, and nobody is tempted to inflate it because it is obviously crude. The judgement about whether a cycle is overloaded now happens in conversation between people who know the work, which is where it was always actually happening anyway, minus the ritual that pretended otherwise.

Deployment is triggered by pushing an annotated tag, not by merging to the default branch. `.github/workflows/release.yml` runs on `push: tags: 'v*'`; the merge workflow builds and publishes an image and then stops. The separation was deliberate. Green main and shippable are different claims, and conflating them meant every merge carried release-sized anxiety, which made people merge less often and in bigger chunks. It also gives us exactly one auditable object per release: the tag, the artifact and the workflow run all line up, so when someone asks what shipped on a given date the answer is a tag name rather than an archaeology exercise across merge commits. Two internal-only services still auto-deploy on merge, because there the tightness of the feedback loop is worth more than the ceremony. Tags are created by the release owner through the release script, never from the web UI, so the annotation always carries the generated changelog body.

Switched trace sampling from head-based to tail-based in `deploy/otel/otel-collector-config.yaml`. Head sampling at two percent was cheap and useless: the traces we wanted during an incident were exactly the ones the dice had thrown away, and asking someone to reproduce a failure so it might get sampled is not a debugging workflow. The tail sampler buffers a trace for ten seconds after the last span, then applies policies in order — keep everything with an error status, keep anything whose root span exceeds one second, keep everything from the two tenant IDs on the migration watchlist, and otherwise `sampling_percentage: 2`. Net storage went up about 30 percent because errors are structurally larger traces, which we accepted as the price of the traces being useful.

The cost is collector memory: the buffer holds every in-flight trace, so a burst of long-running route solves pushed the collector into repeated restarts until we raised the decision cache and capped `num_traces`. That is now the first thing to check if spans go missing during a slow period — it is almost never the SDK, it is the collector evicting under buffer pressure.

Configured the long-term metric store with three resolution tiers: `--retention.resolution-raw=15d`, `--retention.resolution-5m=90d`, `--retention.resolution-1h=395d`. The 395 rather than 365 is intentional — it means that during the freight peak in late November we can still compare against the same week of the previous year, including a month of margin for someone doing the analysis in December rather than the day of.

Raw at fifteen days covers every debugging use we actually observed; queries older than that are invariably capacity or seasonality questions where five-minute resolution is more than sufficient. The tiers cut object storage roughly in half compared to the previous flat retention.

The gotcha, learned the hard way, is that downsampled series carry aggregate types and a naive rate() over a long window can silently read the 1h blocks and produce a smoother, lower curve than reality. Panels intended for long ranges use the aggregation-aware functions and are labelled as downsampled in the panel description. Anyone quoting a peak value from a range over ninety days should be treated with suspicion unless they checked which tier answered the query.

Put a review gate in front of third-party scripts on the marketing site after finding four tags in the tag manager that nobody could attribute to a current campaign. Marketing owned the tag manager and rightly did not want engineering approval on every experiment, so the compromise is that any script loaded from a domain not already on the allowlist requires a short review, and the allowlist is maintained jointly. The enforcement is a content security policy header rather than a process promise, which means a tag added outside the allowlist simply doesn't load and marketing finds out immediately rather than three weeks later. The policy is defined in `edge/csp_policy.conf` and the allowlist portion is a separate included file so marketing can propose changes without touching the rest. We deliberately did not extend this to the application itself, which loads no third-party scripts at all and has a much stricter policy — conflating the two would have produced a policy too loose for the app in order to be workable for the site. Two separate policies, two separate owners, documented reasoning for the difference.

A written proposal stays open for comment for three working days, and silence at the end of the window counts as consent. Anyone who needs more time says so in the thread and gets it — asking is enough, no justification required — but not asking and objecting afterwards is out of order. Three days is calibrated to the spread across Lisbon, Berlin and Halifax plus a normal amount of vacation: it survives one person being out for a long weekend without stalling everything behind them. The rule mostly protects proposals from dying of ambient uncertainty, which was the real failure mode before. Nobody was blocking anything; authors simply never knew whether they were allowed to proceed, so half-agreed proposals sat unimplemented for weeks and were rediscovered later by someone solving the same problem from scratch.

Every engineer posts a written update by end of day Thursday in their team channel, and the leads fold the four team notes into one org-wide note whose format is pinned in `handbook/rituals/thursday-note.md`. The cap is five lines: what shipped, what is stuck, what changed for someone else, what you need. It ships even in a week where nothing moved — "blocked on the same review as last week" is a legitimate and useful note, and suppressing it is how a two-week stall becomes invisible. The rule exists because Lisbon, Berlin and Halifax share barely three hours of overlap, so anything that depends on being in a room at the right moment reaches maybe half the team. A written note is read at whatever hour suits the reader, is searchable six months later when an incident review asks when a behaviour started, and takes four minutes to write. Leads are explicitly told not to editorialise the team notes into progress narratives — the roll-up is a concatenation with duplicates removed, not a status report.

Convention is one tmux session per repo, named after the repo directory. The shared `~/.tmux.conf` sets `set -g base-index 1` so window numbers line up with the keyboard, turns on `set -g mouse on` (contested, kept, because pairing with someone who cannot scroll is worse than purity), and keeps the default prefix so that helping someone in their own session does not require relearning it. The wrapper is a shell function `tm` that runs `tmux new-session -As "$(basename "$PWD")"`, which attaches if the session exists and creates it otherwise, so you never end up with three detached sessions for the same project. The point of naming sessions after repos is that a dev server, a test watcher and a shell for one project stay together and survive laptop sleep, VPN drops and terminal app restarts. Before this, people ran everything in stacked terminal tabs and lost their whole layout roughly weekly, usually while trying to reproduce something.

There is a soak period before a tool joins the shared baseline: someone has to have used it on their own machine for a full quarter and still want it. This is not conservatism for its own sake. The last three rewritten-in-a-faster-language command line replacements we adopted enthusiastically all delivered exactly what they promised, and two of them still cost us about a week each in migration, documentation, and the long tail of people whose muscle memory kept invoking the old thing. The failure mode we are guarding against is a baseline that churns faster than anyone can learn it, where the setup doc is subtly wrong because it describes last quarter's stack. Personal use is unconstrained and encouraged; the constraint applies only to what everyone is expected to have installed and what the docs are allowed to assume. In practice the soak period filters well — roughly half the tools someone was excited enough to propose were quietly abandoned within a month, without anyone having to argue against them.

A single `.tool-versions` file at each repo root pins the Go, Node and Python versions, and both the local dev shell and the CI setup step read it rather than each naming a version of their own. Before this, the workflow named one Go version and the README named another, and the gap was discovered by a build failure that only appeared on a colleague's machine three weeks after the drift started. The setup step in CI now takes no version argument at all, which is the property we actually wanted: one place to change it, and changing it changes both. The dependency bot opens bump pull requests against `.tool-versions`, so the resulting CI run is a genuine test of the upgrade rather than a rubber stamp on a number nobody executed.

Trace context now survives the event bus. Producers write `traceparent` into the message headers and consumers extract it in the shared wrapper at `pkg/eventbus/tracing.go`, so a driver check-in can be followed from the ingest HTTP span through the topic and into the settlement worker in one view. Before this, every asynchronous hop was a dead end and correlating them meant grepping for a request ID by hand.

The design decision worth remembering is that the consumer span is a link, not a child. Making it a child produced traces that stayed open for as long as the consumer lag — during the morning surge that was minutes — and the backend either dropped them or reported wall-clock durations that described queueing, not work. Links keep each side's timing honest while preserving navigability.

Batch consumers get one span per batch with a link per message, capped at 128 links, because a thousand-message batch produced spans large enough to be rejected by the collector's payload limit. If someone is chasing a message that vanished, the first thing to check is whether it was in an oversized batch that hit the link cap.

`TRACKING_BATCH_SIZE = 500` in the ingest consumer, and it is a measured number rather than a round one. Benchmarked 100, 500, and 2000 against a day of replayed carrier traffic. At 100 most of the time went to per-batch overhead and round trips. At 2000 throughput was marginally better, but the batch held row locks long enough that the API's own writes to `tracking_events` started queueing behind it, and a mid-batch failure meant redoing twenty times as much work. 500 lands at about ninety-four percent of peak throughput with worst-case redo well under a second. One more thing that mattered: the insert path builds a single parameter list per batch, and 2000 put us close to the wire protocol's parameter limit for the widest row shape, which would have become an interesting outage months later. If the row shape grows, re-run the benchmark rather than assuming the number still holds.

Added a license check to the dependency pipeline after legal flagged that we had no idea what was in our transitive tree. The check is not a blocker on unknown licenses — that produced immediate revolt when we tried it — but it does block a specific deny list of strongly copyleft licenses in anything that ships to customers, while permitting them in build tooling that never leaves our infrastructure. The distinction is encoded as two separate allowlists keyed on whether the dependency group is `runtime` or `dev`. Config lives in `tools/license_policy.toml`. Unknown or unparseable licenses generate a warning and a line in the weekly report rather than a failure, on the theory that a warning somebody reads beats an error somebody suppresses. We seeded the exception list from the existing tree rather than trying to fix everything at once, and gave each exception a review date so the list shrinks rather than grows. Twelve of the original forty-one exceptions have since been cleared, mostly by upstream projects clarifying their own metadata. The remaining ones are genuinely ambiguous and legal has looked at each.

We support macOS and Linux laptops as first-class development environments and pay the cost of doing so. The cost is real: every setup instruction has two branches, the container runtime differs, and the file-watching behaviour is different enough that a bug reproducing on one and not the other has burned an afternoon more than once. We keep it because the engineer who maintains the edge agent needs to develop against the same kernel features the agent uses in the field, and because two of our best hires arrived with Linux laptops and no appetite for switching. What we explicitly do not support is Windows without the Linux subsystem; that came up with a contractor, and the answer was to run everything inside the subsystem rather than try to make the toolchain native. The line we drew is that both supported platforms must work from the documented setup path with no undocumented local knowledge. If something only works because a particular person remembers a fix, that is a bug in the setup docs, not a quirk of the platform.

Python environments live at `.venv` in the repo root, created and managed by uv, gitignored, never shared between repos. `uv sync --frozen` is what `make bootstrap` runs, and `uv run pytest` is how tests start, so nobody has to think about whether the environment is activated in this particular shell. The location matters more than the tool: with `.venv` at the root, every editor we support — VS Code, Neovim with basedpyright, PyCharm for the one holdout — finds the interpreter with zero configuration. The previous convention put environments in a central directory keyed by project name, and the recurring failure was the language server quietly falling back to the system interpreter, producing type errors and completions that were subtly wrong in ways people did not immediately notice. Moving to uv from pip-tools was a speed decision layered on top of that: a cold environment build went from roughly ninety seconds to under ten, which is the difference between rebuilding an environment the moment you suspect it and living with a suspicious one for a week.

Established that any external vendor or contractor access to our systems is created with an expiry from the outset, never open-ended, and that the expiry is set to the contract end date or ninety days, whichever is sooner. This came out of discovering an active account belonging to a consultancy whose engagement had finished eighteen months earlier. Nobody had done anything wrong; there was simply no step in the offboarding process that touched external identities, because external identities were created ad hoc by whoever was sponsoring the work. Now the sponsor is recorded on the account, the sponsor gets a reminder a week before expiry, and renewal requires them to affirm the engagement is ongoing. The renewal rate is around forty percent, which tells you how much of the previous state was inertia. The part that took negotiation was the vendors themselves, some of whom found the re-request cycle irritating and said so. We held the line because the alternative is trusting a third party's offboarding process to protect our systems, and we have no visibility into that process at all. Two vendors now proactively tell us when their staff rotate, which is more than we got before.

Every service binary embeds its build metadata through ldflags — `-X main.buildSHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD)` plus the tag when there is one — and exposes it at `/internal/version`. This exists because of a bad half hour during an incident when nobody could say with confidence which build was serving traffic: the deployment object said one thing, the registry tag was ambiguous, and the answer eventually came from someone remembering what they had rolled out on Tuesday. Now the first step in any investigation is to curl the version endpoint on the affected pods and compare. The endpoint deliberately returns nothing beyond sha, tag and build time. Requests to add dependency versions and feature state were declined, to keep it a boring stable contract that is present in every service including the two oldest ones nobody wants to touch.

`.vscode/settings.json` is committed in each repo, and the rule we agreed on is that it may contain only settings which would break the repo if they were wrong: `"editor.formatOnSave": true`, the per-language formatter binding, `"python.defaultInterpreterPath": ".venv/bin/python"`, and `files.exclude` entries hiding `.venv` and build output so the file picker stays usable. Themes, font sizes, keybindings and anything else that is taste stay in user settings and are explicitly out of scope for review. `.vscode/extensions.json` carries recommendations only — the editor prompts once and nobody is blocked if they decline. We also committed a single `launch.json` debug configuration for the API, because attaching a debugger was the one setup step people quietly skipped, and a working F5 on day one visibly changed how often the debugger got used at all. The alternative, gitignoring the whole `.vscode` directory, is what we did before, and it meant every new VS Code user spent their first hour rediscovering the same four settings.

Agreed a filter for the paging rotation: if the honest answer to "would we fix this at three in the morning" is no, it does not page. It goes to a ticket queue that gets looked at in the morning. This sounds obvious and was not how we operated. We had a substantial category of alerts about slowly-filling resources and degraded-but-working conditions that woke people up so they could acknowledge and go back to sleep, which is the worst possible outcome — the cost of the interruption with none of the benefit. Applying the filter moved about a quarter of our alert definitions to the daytime queue. The objection was that some of those conditions eventually become the three-in-the-morning kind, and that's true, so the ones with a trajectory got a second threshold much closer to the actual cliff, and only that second threshold pages. The first threshold is now a ticket. Sleep quality on the rotation improved enough that two people mentioned it unprompted, and we have not yet had a case where a daytime-queue item escalated into an outage before anyone looked at it.

Made signature verification mandatory on every inbound webhook endpoint, including the ones we assumed were unreachable. The trigger was finding a partner integration endpoint that had been live for two years with no verification at all, protected only by an obscure URL. Anyone who had ever seen that URL in a log line could have posted arbitrary events into our order pipeline. We wrote a shared verifier so nobody hand-rolls the comparison, because the two endpoints that did verify were both using a non-constant-time string compare. It lives in `halyard/http/webhook_verify.py` and exposes a single decorator; endpoints that don't use it are caught by a lint rule that greps for the route registration pattern and requires the decorator on the same function. Timestamp tolerance is `max_skew_seconds = 300`, which was picked to survive one partner's occasionally lagging queue and is deliberately not configurable per-endpoint so nobody quietly widens it. Two partners had to be contacted because they weren't signing at all; one shipped signing in a week, the other took four months and we ran their endpoint on an allowlisted source range in the meantime.

Retired the VPN as the gate for internal web tools and moved to an identity-aware proxy in front of each service. The VPN had become a soft perimeter that people were inside of for eight hours a day regardless of what they were doing, which meant a compromised laptop had network reach to everything on the internal ranges. The proxy checks identity and group membership per request, so a laptop that gets popped can only reach the tools that person was already entitled to, and we get a per-request audit trail we never had before. The migration took longer than planned mostly because three tools assumed they were the only thing on their host and served on paths that collided. The VPN still exists for direct database access and for the couple of appliances that can't sit behind HTTP auth, but it is no longer the default way anyone reaches anything. Notably, this also killed the habit of sharing an internal URL in chat and expecting the recipient to just open it — now they either have access or they get a clear denial page telling them which group to request. That friction turned out to be a feature.

Workers get `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 90` and a SIGTERM handler that cancels the broker consumer first, finishes whatever is in flight, then closes the channel and exits. Kubernetes' thirty-second default was killing label renders mid-carrier-call, which left us paying for a label we never delivered and requeuing a job the carrier had already fulfilled. Order matters more than the number: stop consuming before you start draining, otherwise the worker keeps accepting new work throughout its own shutdown and never actually finishes. The ninety seconds is p99 task duration plus margin, so it needs revisiting whenever the slowest task class gets slower. `notify-worker` keeps the default, because its tasks are milliseconds long and a generous grace period would only slow deploys down. Useful during incidents: a rolling deploy of the label workers takes about six minutes end to end because of this, and that is the design working, not the deploy being stuck.

Whoever writes a row owns invalidating the cache entries derived from it. We tried the opposite for about a year — readers defending themselves with short TTLs everywhere — and it produced the worst of both worlds: staleness still long enough for customers to notice, and a read rate high enough that the cache was barely earning its keep. Putting invalidation next to the write means there is exactly one place to look when something is stale, and it is the same place that changed. It does force the writing service to know which derived keys exist, which is a real coupling and not a free one, and it is the reason key construction lives in shared code rather than being spelled out at each call site. Where the write happens outside our services — a vendor changing something on their side without telling us — the honest answer is that a TTL is all we have, and those particular TTLs are deliberately short.

Incident write-ups refer to roles rather than individuals — the on-duty engineer, the reviewer, the author of the change — even when everyone reading knows exactly who is meant. The convention was adopted after an early write-up named someone in the timeline and then circulated well outside engineering, where it was read by people with no context for how normal the mistake had been. Nothing bad happened to that person, but the next few write-ups were noticeably more defensive and less useful, which is the cost we are actually protecting against. The related habit: describe what the system did in the present tense and what people did in the past tense, and never write that someone should have known. If it was knowable at the time from the information they had, that is a finding about the information, not about them.

Shell startup has a budget: `zsh -i -c exit` must stay under 250ms on a current laptop, measured with hyperfine, and the dotfiles CI job fails if it regresses past 400ms. The number is not arbitrary. A standard tmux layout opens six panes, and a 900ms rc file — which is where we were before the cleanup — turns attaching into a visible multi-second stall every single time. The wins came from three changes: running `compinit` against a cached dump and rebuilding it only when the completion files are newer, deferring the cloud CLI completion scripts behind lazy stub functions that replace themselves on first call, and moving syntax highlighting to the very end of the rc where it has to be anyway. `zprof` stays commented out at the top and bottom of the rc with a note explaining how to enable both halves, because the next person investigating a slow shell should not have to rediscover that trick. The plugin manager was never the problem and we did not switch away from it.
